candidates.title: Fostering Emotional Engagement and Sustained Interaction in Care Homes Through Empathetic Human–Robot Conversation
candidates.abstract: Social isolation is a critical health concern for older adults—especially in institutional care, where limited social interaction is linked with depression, cognitive decline and poorer physical health. Empathetic human–robot interaction offers a promising avenue to address these emotional and mental health challenges. We report on a two-stage evaluation of an LLM-powered social robot designed to support emotionally attuned conversations with older adults. In a lab study ( \(N=40\) ), the robot achieved high scores on four empathy-related measures. We then deployed a fully autonomous system for 10 weeks in a residential care home (five residents; up to 45 minutes per session). Across repeated interactions, participants showed sustained engagement and predominantly mid-depth self-disclosure, alongside affective trust and occasional cognitive trust. Exploratory analyses indicated that higher empathic appropriateness co-occurred with deeper disclosure and increased over sessions for most participants. To our knowledge, these findings provide early field evidence that autonomous, LLM-driven conversational robots can maintain emotionally supportive dialogue with older adults, fostering emotional engagement, trust and sustained interaction over time, mechanisms that may contribute to reducing perceived social isolation.

candidates.title: Human-inspired Route Selection for Efficient Social Robot Navigation in Narrow Spaces
candidates.abstract: Narrow human environments are challenging for social robot navigation, where distance-optimal shortcut routes to destination are frequently blocked by people in the aisles. People in these situations select the appropriate route between detour and shortcut in an efficient and socially-aware way, by balancing their extra effort (if choosing detour) and the required effort from the person on the way to make space to pass. Similar balance strategy is utilized when people decide the politeness of the request utterance to compensate for the way yielding effort from others. Inspired by this human balance strategy, we developed a decision-making methodological framework for socially-aware high-level path planning and interaction utterance when the robot navigates in narrow shared spaces and implemented it onto a humanoid mobile robot. In order to demonstrate the transparency and utility of this framework, we present a specific instantiation by conducting a set of human-robot experiments in a real store. Data from 30 people were collected via two field experiments to identify socially-acceptable parameters. Results of a within-participants study with 28 human customers interestingly demonstrated that the proposed socially-aware method was more time-efficient compared to the detour-only and shortcut-only strategies.

candidates.title: Gaze estimation for social robotics
candidates.abstract: A single glance can say a lot. It can show interest, attract attention, hint at what someone wants, or regulate turn-taking. Humans use gaze naturally in social life, and as social robots enter hospitals, classrooms, and public spaces, they need to understand this silent language too. A robot with eyes and a face that ignores gaze, or responds at the wrong moment, can feel strange and lose people’s trust. Accurate gaze estimation has traditionally relied on specialized hardware such as dedi- cated eye trackers, which are often expensive, intrusive, and difficult to deploy in natural human-robot interaction. This thesis asks whether appearance-based gaze estimation models, which infer gaze from ordinary camera images of faces, can offer a practical alternative for social robots. I evaluated appearance-based gaze estimation models against eye trackers and manual annotation, and tested them in human-robot interaction settings. The results show that within 2 meters, these models are already useful when model choice, camera resolution, and calibration are handled well. They can partly replace manual annotation and, with simple correction, match eye trackers for average gaze patterns, though fast attention shifts remain difficult to capture. I also found that tablets can increase task engagement but may also distract users. Finally, I built a real-time task-completion detection system, showing that effective gaze interaction is possible on standard robots using low-cost devices. Overall, this thesis demonstrates that AI-based gaze estimation cannot yet read minds and remains far from perfect. Still, it can serve as a practical component of human-robot interaction when gaze signals are interpreted in relation to task-specific social meaning, and when experimental design and parameter selection are carefully tailored. Future research should extend these capabilities to real-world and multi-user environments and integrate gaze with speech, gesture, and vision-language models, bringing gaze-aware robots closer to seamless social interaction in everyday settings.

candidates.title: Multimodal Voice Activity Projection for Social Robot Mediation: Expected Behavior and Deployment Constraints
candidates.abstract: Turn-taking prediction is especially relevant for social robots that act as mediators in human-human interaction, where the expected action is often not to speak, but to orient, wait, avoid interruption, or prepare a balanced intervention. This paper presents Multimodal Voice Activity Projection (MM-VAP) as a human state-aware perception layer for future robot mediation behavior. The model estimates the future evolution of the conversational floor from synchronized audio-visual evidence and derives turn-taking events such as Hold, Shift, Shift prediction, Backchannel prediction, and overlap-related states. The approach uses VA-related pretrained audio-visual encoders, LoRA adaptation, inter-speaker attention, and zero-shot event inference from future voice activity projections. Experiments on NoXi, NoXi+J, and Haru EDR support the feasibility of this formulation, especially for floor management events that can be connected to gaze preparation, active listening, and conservative intervention. Finally, the paper defines the expected robot output interface and discusses the main deployment constraints, including real-time inference, preprocessing latency, multimodal synchronization, and input-quality monitoring.

candidates.title: Supporting Social Engagement in Long-Term Care Through Paired Socially Assistive Robot-Virtual Reality Activities for Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment and Apathy
candidates.abstract: Miroslava Migovich,1 Ritam Ghosh,2 Nibraas Khan,3 Cathy A Maxwell,4 Paul A Newhouse,5 Douglas W Scharre,6 Alai Tan,7 Judith A Tate,7,* Lorraine C Mion,7,* Nilanjan Sarkar1– 3,*1Department of Mechanical Engineering, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA; 2Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA; 3Department of Computer Science, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA; 4College of Nursing, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA; 5Center for Cognitive Medicine, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN, USA; 6Department of Neurology, The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, Columbus, OH, USA; 7College of Nursing, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA*These authors contributed equally to this workCorrespondence: Miroslava Migovich, Department of Mechanical Engineering, Vanderbilt University, 2400 Highland Ave, Room 107, Nashville, TN, 37212, USA, Email miroslava.migovich@vanderbilt.eduIntroduction: Older adults living in long-term care settings, particularly those with cognitive impairment and apathy, frequently experience reduced social engagement. Socially assistive robots and virtual reality systems may help support engagement, but little is known about whether they can sustain engagement during real-world deployment while also facilitating interaction between older adults. This study examined whether socially structured socially assistive robot-virtual reality (SAR-VR) systems could sustain engagement and support human-human interaction during repeated use in long-term care settings.Methods: This analysis focused on the SAR-VR intervention arm of a larger eight-week study and included 60 older adults with cognitive impairment from 23 long-term care sites. Participants were exposed to two SAR-VR systems featuring different robot embodiments (dog-like and humanoid), roles, and activities. Across 756 repeated intervention sessions, engagement was observationally assessed using observed ratings of attention, activity attitude, robot attitude, and conversational targeting.Results: Sustained attention and activity attitudes remained consistently positive across both SAR-VR systems over repeated exposure. Peer-to-peer and research-staff directed speech occurred across both systems. While robot-directed speech was more common in the dog-like condition, partner-directed communication remained stable, indicating that increased human-robot interaction did not occur at the expense of human–human interaction. Baseline cognitive functioning was associated with attentional engagement but not with attitudinal evaluations. Baseline technology acceptance did not strongly predict post-interaction impressions. Participants who anthropomorphized the robots at baseline demonstrated more positive engagement during sessions.Discussion: These findings suggest that socially structured SAR-VR systems can sustain meaningful engagement while preserving peer interaction in naturalistic dementia care. The results also support the feasibility of designing SAR-VR activities around shared goals and coordinated actions to promote reciprocal human engagement, while recognizing that the study design does not allow definitive conclusions about clinical efficacy or the effects of specific robot features.Keywords: collaborative technologies, multimodal intervention, human-centered design, dyadic activities, cognitive impairment, apathy

candidates.title: MultiTalk: Scaling Full-Duplex Speech Models to Long, Multi-Party, Bilingual Conversation
candidates.abstract: End-to-end full-duplex speech models have brought open-source machine conversation closer to human-like interaction, yet existing systems remain limited in two intertwined dimensions: long-context robustness and multi-party interaction. Real-world scenarios such as meetings, group lessons, and social-robot reception require a single model to track, contextualize, and respond to multiple speakers over extended durations. Progress is constrained by both data and evaluation: open multi-party speech corpora remain small and are not designed for codec-frame-level full-duplex modeling, while existing long-audio benchmarks focus on passive listening and speech-to-speech benchmarks are mostly short and dyadic. We extend the Moshi paradigm jointly along the long-horizon and multi-party axes in English and Chinese. First, we release 57.6k hours of synthetic training data ($\href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/MultiTalk/MultiTalkPT}{MultiTalkPT}$ and $\href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/MultiTalk/MultiTalkFT}{MultiTalkFT}$) for long-form, multi-party, English-Chinese full-duplex dialogue, with controllable length, participant count, turn-taking, overlap, backchannels, interruptions, addressee shifts, and long-range coreference. Second, we introduce $\href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/MultiTalk/MultiTalkBench}{MultiTalkBench}$, built from real human recordings, for evaluating long-form, multi-party, bilingual full-duplex dialogue. Conversations average 32.6 minutes and include probes for long-range entity tracking, topic coherence, and addressee selection. Third, we train a bilingual Moshi-style model that sustains coherent multi-party English-Chinese conversations over extended durations and substantially outperforms open-source baselines including Moshi, MiniCPM-o-4.5, and Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct on MultiTalkBench.

candidates.title: Supporting Social Engagement in Long-Term Care Through Paired Socially Assistive Robot-Virtual Reality Activities for Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment and Apathy
candidates.abstract: Introduction: Older adults living in long-term care settings, particularly those with cognitive impairment and apathy, frequently experience reduced social engagement. Socially assistive robots and virtual reality systems may help support engagement, but little is known about whether they can sustain engagement during real-world deployment while also facilitating interaction between older adults. This study examined whether socially structured socially assistive robot-virtual reality (SAR-VR) systems could sustain engagement and support human-human interaction during repeated use in long-term care settings. Methods: This analysis focused on the SAR-VR intervention arm of a larger eight-week study and included 60 older adults with cognitive impairment from 23 long-term care sites. Participants were exposed to two SAR-VR systems featuring different robot embodiments (dog-like and humanoid), roles, and activities. Across 756 repeated intervention sessions, engagement was observationally assessed using observed ratings of attention, activity attitude, robot attitude, and conversational targeting. Results: Sustained attention and activity attitudes remained consistently positive across both SAR-VR systems over repeated exposure. Peer-to-peer and research-staff directed speech occurred across both systems. While robot-directed speech was more common in the dog-like condition, partner-directed communication remained stable, indicating that increased human-robot interaction did not occur at the expense of human-human interaction. Baseline cognitive functioning was associated with attentional engagement but not with attitudinal evaluations. Baseline technology acceptance did not strongly predict post-interaction impressions. Participants who anthropomorphized the robots at baseline demonstrated more positive engagement during sessions. Discussion: These findings suggest that socially structured SAR-VR systems can sustain meaningful engagement while preserving peer interaction in naturalistic dementia care. The results also support the feasibility of designing SAR-VR activities around shared goals and coordinated actions to promote reciprocal human engagement, while recognizing that the study design does not allow definitive conclusions about clinical efficacy or the effects of specific robot features.

candidates.title: Gestures for Human-Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Human interaction involves the interplay of various communication media, including body movements, voice, gaze, and even written signs. In such an interplay, gestures and, more generally, body motions represent a fundamental communication channel. Due to the significance of gesture-based communication in human-human interaction, intelligent and embodied agents are expected to utilize its implications to interact with humans effectively. An embodied agent, like a robot, can reason and produce gestures as a bidirectional communication channel between itself and the human it is interacting with. To achieve full bidirectional, gesture-based communication, the same embodied agent should be able to both recognize and perform communicative and informative gestures. This chapter describes the different challenges characterizing gesture-based interaction models between humans and robots.

candidates.title: Emotional chain reasoning-driven multimodal fusion for empathic humanoid robot interaction
candidates.abstract: As humanoid robots enter companion service, educational assistance, rehabilitation support, and public interaction, the central challenge is not only to recognize emotion but to convert multimodal human cues into coordinated language and action. The proposed Emotional Chain Reasoning-Driven Multimodal Fusion Network (ECDT-MFN) is not a separate alternative to vision-language-action (VLA) architectures. At the task and pipeline level, it is an emotion-aware VLA extension: visual observations and language context are mapped to social actions, while voice prosody, facial expression, body movement, and haptic feedback provide an auxiliary biometric-affective observation stream. The contribution lies in adding dynamic affective conditioning, explicit-to-implicit emotional chain reasoning, and empathy-conditioned action planning to this VLA-style perception-language-action loop. The model jointly produces empathic verbal responses and executable social behaviors such as gaze, head posture, interaction distance, waiting, assistance, and conflict avoidance. Evaluation is therefore organized at two levels. Participant-centered, end-to-end HRI outcomes—including perceived empathy, behavioral appropriateness, user satisfaction, interaction continuity, and long-term consistency—serve as the primary evidence of effectiveness; automatic emotion-recognition, semantic-similarity, module-ablation, and noise-retention measures are retained only as diagnostic evidence. Results show that the complete emotion-aware VLA pipeline improves the tested whole-interaction outcomes while maintaining the measured software-inference latency of the reference implementation. These findings support the value of affective conditioning for socially responsive VLA control, rather than claiming a new non-VLA control paradigm.

candidates.title: RoboCafé in the Open: Interaction Continuity in Long-Term Public Human-Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: As robots remain in public spaces over extended periods, they must maintain interaction continuity by preserving and correctly applying context as people, encounters, and circumstances change. To study interaction continuity in long-term public human-robot interactions, we developed RoboCafé, an autonomous conversational coffee robot designed to support repeated interactions through task-aware dialogue, real-time multimodal perception, and memory of prior encounters. We deployed RoboCafé for 12 days in a university building, where it received 148 orders. The deployment involved repeat customers, passersby, changing groups, and back-to-back orders that repeatedly crossed the boundaries assumed by the system's order-centered interaction model. We found that successful interaction continuity requires a robot to determine who is currently present, which prior context belongs to whom, where interactions begin and end, and whether its representation of an interaction matches what is occurring in the physical world. From these observations, we derive four system design requirements for maintaining interaction continuity in longitudinal public human-robot interactions: contextual interaction state, persistent person grounding, explicit interaction life-cycle management, and interaction observability.

candidates.title: Towards an Extensible Benchmark for Spoken Dialogue with Social Robots
candidates.abstract: Language models provide a plug-and-play interface between humans and robots, but important challenges remain when speech, dialogue, fast interaction, and collaboration are required. We propose a benchmark for the community to use as a way to explore common spoken dialogue artifacts between robots and humans, including requests for clarification, interruptions, embodied signals (e.g., head nods or facial cues), and time constraints. We also explain our vision to extend the benchmark for other aspects of human-robot interaction that are important to the larger research community. To facilitate the benchmark, we further propose using \textit{Retico}, a real-time communication framework that fulfills important technical requirements to enable robots to have spoken dialogue capabilities.

candidates.title: Trustworthy agricultural autonomy integrates robot learning safe control and human robot interaction
candidates.abstract: The future of modern farming is intelligent, autonomous and data-driven farming operations. This will help to address the increasing labor shortage, resource constraints and climate variability. But for deployment in unstructured agricultural settings, high-performance automation is needed, as well as trustworthy systems that can make safe decisions, have the ability to learn adaptively and collaborate effectively with human operators. In this review, we discuss recent progress in trustworthy agricultural autonomy from the perspective of three interrelated pillars: robot learning and perception, safe control and resilient planning, and human-robot interaction. This review surveys state-of-the-art perception technologies such as computer vision, LiDAR, sensor fusion and deep reinforcement learning and safety-oriented approaches including model predictive control, formal verification, failure management and resilient navigation. It also addresses human-robot collaborative systems, explainable AI, ergonomics safety and sustainability-aware robotic design and discusses ethical, regulatory and socio-economic issues related to autonomous farming. Commercial applications of autonomous weeding, robotic harvesting and broad-acre field operations are now in existence, providing real-world demonstrations of the use of these technologies, and their potential to increase productivity, improve resource efficiency and enhance environmental sustainability. Finally, the review wraps up by underlining some future research priorities like universal safety certification, edge computing, interoperability, swarm robotics, and digital twin integration. Collectively, the reviewed evidence identifies the technical, human, and governance requirements that must be addressed to support safer, more resilient, transparent, and sustainable deployment of autonomous agricultural systems. candidates.title: Calm beats cute: designing aesthetic-functional congruence in human-robot interaction for breathing companion robots
candidates.abstract: Introduction: Which robot would you trust to guide you through a breathing exercise, a cute cartoon-like humanoid, a soft animal companion, a clinical mechanical device, or a serene meditative figure? This study examines how four design aesthetics affect social evaluation and technology acceptance of Neffy, a social breathing-companion robot that supports stress relief and wellbeing by guiding exercises through visual, audio, and haptic cues synchronized with upper-body movement. Methods: In an online study, 126 participants viewed a video of a person interacting with Neffy during a guided breathing exercise. Four design styles were tested: cartoonish humanoid, meditative humanoid, animal-like (zoomorphic), and machine-like (mechanomorphic). Participants rated each style on warmth, competence, perceived enjoyment, and intention to use, and made pairwise comparisons of human-likeness, social presence, trustworthiness, breathing companion preference, and overall liking. Results: The zoomorphic design received the highest warmth ratings, the mechanomorphic design scored lowest across all measures. Perceived human-likeness positively predicted both warmth and competence, confirming its role in social evaluation. However, human-likeness alone did not determine preference: despite comparable perceived human-likeness between the two humanoid designs, the meditative humanoid achieved the highest scores for competence, trustworthiness, and breathing companion preference, outperforming the cartoon-like humanoid. Discussion: These results suggest that "calm" aesthetics are preferred over "cute" aesthetics for wellbeing robots, challenging the assumption that human-likeness alone drives design success. Instead, aesthetic-functional congruence-alignment between a robot's visual design and its functional purpose, appears to be a critical, under-explored factor in social robot design for wellbeing. Since this study assessed general evaluations, future work should test whether these preferences hold across application domains (e.g. clinical, workplace, educational, domestic) and cross-cultural contexts.

candidates.title: Enabling Quechua speech in humanoid social robots through fine-tuned neural TTS on the UBTech Walker Tienkung
candidates.abstract: Humanoid social robots deployed in multilingual societies-particularly in indigenous communities-face a critical linguistic gap: their speech interfaces are predominantly designed for high-resource languages, excluding hundreds of millions of indigenous language speakers from equitable human-robot interaction. This study presents the first neural text-to-speech (TTS) system for Southern Quechua-the most extensive indigenous language family of the Americas, with more than ten million active speakers-deployed on a humanoid social robot. XTTS-v2, a multilingual neural TTS model, was fine-tuned on 22,727 validated utterances (30.5 h, 77 speakers) of the Cusco-Puno dialect, located in southern Peru, through a tokenizer adaptation that leverages the phonological overlap between Quechua and Spanish. Fine-tuning over 15 epochs on an NVIDIA A100 40 GB GPU achieved a 35.0% reduction in training cross-entropy loss (4.084 → 2.652), confirming effective adaptation to Quechua phonology and morphology with stable training dynamics across 35,000 gradient update steps. Inference latency was evaluated on two hardware environments: the training GPU (mean latency: 2,037 ms; Real-Time Factor (RTF) = 0.472) and the embedded SoC of the UBTech Walker Tienkung humanoid robot (Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB; mean latency: 5,913 ms; RTF = 0.961). Both configurations achieved a mean RTF below 1.0, demonstrating real-time Quechua speech synthesis directly on the robot's hardware without external computing infrastructure. Intelligibility evaluation using Whisper large-v3 with automatic language detection yielded a Word Error Rate of 147.4% and a Character Error Rate of 69.1%; these values reflect the absence of a native Quechua automatic speech recognition (ASR) model rather than the quality of TTS synthesis. These results establish the first quantitative benchmark for TTS in American indigenous languages on a humanoid robotic platform and provide a reproducible framework-encompassing training configuration, tokenizer adaptation, and deployment pipeline-for extending neural speech synthesis to other low-resource languages of the Americas.

candidates.title: Designing and Evaluating Socially Assistive Robots: The Role of Language Choice in Dementia Care Scenarios
candidates.abstract: Language plays a central role in person-centered care, shaping communication, emotional expression, memory recall, and identity. While socially assistive robots (SAR) show promise for reminiscence-based activities in dementia care, most systems remain monolingual and overlook bilingual users. This work investigated how language choice in SAR interactions influenced engagement, emotional experience, and user perception among Turkish-German bilingual adults aged 50 and above. An embodied conversational agent based on a Q.bo One robot and a large language model was developed to enable interactions in German and Turkish. A qualitative user study was conducted in which four participants engaged in robot-led reminiscence sessions over a week, with three days per language condition. We situate our findings in the context of linguistic relativity and symbolic interactionism theories; and propose design considerations for linguistically adaptive SAR.

candidates.title: How to express social presence: a comparison of perceptions of social robots’ cognitive abilities
candidates.abstract: In light of the problems posed by an aging society and the associated challenges-particularly regarding the care and support of older citizens-questions arise concerning technological solutions. Social robots equipped with appropriate cognitive abilities can provide support in this area by reducing loneliness and social isolation through communication and personalized interaction. To this end, the robot's perceived social presence is of crucial importance. Social presence (or co-presence) refers to the sense of being with another person and depends on how easily one feels able to access that person's intelligence, intentions, and sensory impressions. This study examined the potential of robots' cognitive abilities for social dialogic interactions with humans, such as (i) unrestricted conversational abilities, (ii) the incorporation of visual cues into interactions, and (iii) memories of individual encounters, and investigates the perceived social presence in each case. In addition, we evaluated the degree of anthropomorphism using the Human-Robot Interaction Evaluation Scale. Our results show a trend toward a higher degree of social presence in terms of visual perception, but only one statistically significant difference out of a total of seven questions on this topic. Memories, as well, had only one statistically significant influence, namely, on the anthropomorphic dimension of disturbance. Gender-specific differences were observed with regard to social presence and the anthropomorphic dimensions. However, these differences are most likely attributable to professional background or certain predispositions rather than to gender itself.

candidates.title: Integrating Theory of Mind into Embodied Agents for Human-Aware Interaction
candidates.abstract: As embodied artificial agents (social robots, virtual assistants, and collaborative manipulators) move from controlled laboratories into homes, hospitals, and workplaces, their ability to interpret and anticipate human mental states becomes as important as their physical competence. This paper presents a unified theoretical and architectural account of how Theory of Mind (ToM), the capacity to attribute beliefs, desires, intentions, and emotions to others, can be integrated into embodied agents to support human-aware interaction. We first formalize a computational notion of ToM suitable for embodied settings, distinguishing zero-order perceptual inference from first- and second-order recursive belief attribution, and we relate these levels to the demands of everyday human-agent collaboration. We then propose a modular architecture, the Belief-Intention-Action (BIA) framework, that couples multimodal perception with a hybrid Bayesian-neural mental-state estimator, a hierarchical intention inference module, and an action-selection policy that explicitly conditions on inferred human mental states. The architecture is instantiated on both a simulated humanoid platform and a physical mobile manipulator and evaluated across three interaction scenarios: collaborative object handover, ambiguous instruction resolution, and false-belief-sensitive assistance. Compared with baseline agents lacking explicit mental-state modeling, the ToM-equipped agent achieves higher task success, faster adaptation to human error, and improved subjective ratings of perceived understanding and comfort, while ablation studies confirm the contribution of second-order reasoning to false-belief tasks. We conclude by discussing implications for trust calibration, the computational cost of recursive mental-state reasoning, and the ethical responsibilities that accompany machines that model human minds.

candidates.title: Social Robotics and Human–Robot Communication
candidates.abstract: This chapter explores the ergonomic, cognitive, and psychological mechanisms underpinning human–robot communication, focusing on the role of social robots in shaping human perception, behaviour, and socio-emotional engagement. By analysing factors such as robot design, embodiment, and communication modalities, the chapter highlights how these elements influence user interaction and the perception of robots as social entities. It examines the integration of verbal and non-verbal communication modalities, addressing challenges in reciprocity and robots’ behavioural appropriateness. The discussion extends to the implications of adaptive technologies like large language models, emphasising the balance between responsiveness and confidentiality in human–robot interactions. Furthermore, the chapter underscores the potential of social robots in workplace and therapeutic settings to enhance efficiency, safety, and emotional well-being of human interactants. By addressing user expectations and ethical considerations, the chapter seeks to provide a comprehensive framework for advancing social robotics applications in fostering meaningful human–robot relationships.

candidates.title: Preclinical evaluation of a safety-aware multimodal robotic pipeline for human–robot interaction in post-stroke rehabilitation
candidates.abstract: Introduction Post-stroke rehabilitation increasingly requires technologies capable of supporting intensive, measurable, and adaptable interventions while preserving clinical supervision and patient safety. This study presents a lightweight, safety-aware, and modular multimodal robotic pipeline for embodied human–robot interaction in post-stroke rehabilitation, with a first target application in hemispatial inattention. Methods The system was implemented on the TIAGo mobile manipulator within a ROS 2-based architecture and integrates therapist-mediated supervision, speech-based and graphical interaction, head-orientation monitoring, adaptive auditory recall, robot-mediated and screen-based task delivery, and structured performance logging. Dialogue management is based on a deterministic finite-state machine coupled with a rule-based Natural Language Understanding pipeline, enabling predictable interaction handling, explicit fallback behavior, and therapist escalation for safety-relevant events. A preliminary preclinical evaluation was conducted in 16 healthy participants, with a repeated acquisition after 1 month. The study assessed operational feasibility, multimodal interaction robustness, head-orientation monitoring stability, task execution, ASR-related interaction events, usability, acceptance, and 1-month reproducibility of workflow execution. Results All participants completed both acquisitions without adverse events or safety-relevant events requiring interruption of the experimental workflow. End-effector recognition accuracy remained high, attention-recall events were infrequent, screen-based visual tasks were successfully administered and logged, and usability and acceptance outcomes were favorable, with low anxiety toward the robotic platform. Discussion These findings support the feasibility of using a therapist-supervised robotic platform as an integrated tool for structured interaction, head-orientation monitoring, rehabilitation-oriented task delivery, and quantitative logging. The study presents a preclinical evaluation of system architecture, safety-aware interaction design, and workflow robustness. Future work is organized in two stages: a dedicated acceptance and robustness protocol in healthy controls to formally test interaction acceptance, speech-recognition robustness, and safety-relevant failure handling, followed by a true rehabilitation protocol in post-stroke patients with hemispatial inattention, including therapist-supervised exercise adaptation.

candidates.title: Pediatric social robotics in ASD: navigating AI blind-spots toward clinical validation
candidates.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into children's therapeutic environments, social robots are emerging as one of the most clinically complex AI applications for pediatric autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This mini-review examines three under-validated "blind-spot" domains: robot-wearable sensor integration, immersive VR-robot hybrid systems, and generative AI conversational interfaces. Although these technologies offer promising opportunities for adaptive and personalized intervention, current evidence remains limited by small pilot studies, insufficient longitudinal validation, and unresolved developmental safety concerns. Key risks include pediatric sensor intolerance, cognitive overload during immersive exposure, privacy concerns related to continuous data collection, and unconstrained AI-generated dialogue that may reinforce maladaptive communicative patterns in vulnerable children. We propose a five-module clinical validation roadmap focused on pediatric calibration standards, standardized developmental outcome measures, multisite randomized controlled trials, longitudinal monitoring, and human-supported safety architectures. CONCLUSION: Adaptive social robotics offers a promising but currently unvalidated frontier in pediatric ASD care. These systems cannot yet be supported as primary therapeutic interventions, as pediatric-specific calibration standards, standardized developmental outcome measures, and adequately powered longitudinal trials remain absent. The proposed validation framework outlines a pathway for ensuring AI-supported interventions augment rather than replace authentic human-centered developmental care. WHAT IS KNOWN: • Social robots can produce measurable short-term gains in social and communication skills in children with autism spectrum disorder. • Supporting evidence derives largely from small, short-duration pilot studies conducted in controlled settings, limiting clinical applicability. WHAT IS NEW: • Three under-validated blind-spot domains are identified: robot-wearable sensor integration, VR-robot hybrid systems, and generative AI conversational interfaces. • A five-module Clinical Validation Roadmap is proposed to move these domains from pilot demonstration toward pediatric standard of care.

candidates.title: Bridging design disciplines: a literature review of biologically-inspired design, human-centered design, and human-robot interaction
candidates.abstract: Abstract As robotic technologies become more integrated into society, there is a growing demand for systems that are not only technically robust, but also socially accepted, safe, and designed for long-term use. Biologically-Inspired Design (BID), Human-Centered Design (HCD), and Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) each offer valuable theories, methodologies, and tools to support the design and evaluation of such systems. Despite their complementary goals, these fields have largely developed in isolation. The lack of integration across BID, HCD, and HRI presents significant barriers for researchers and designers seeking to create biologically-informed, human-centered robots that facilitate meaningful interactions. In this work, an integrative literature review was conducted to examine the fields of BID, HCD, and HRI. An analytic categorization approach was used to categorize 63 papers into one or more of the three fields: 20 in BID, 27 in HCD, and 21 in HRI, with some papers categorized into multiple categories. Within each field, an inductive, interpretive coding and thematic analysis were used to identify key terminology, tools, methods, and conceptual frameworks, helping establish a shared vocabulary and summarize the state of the art. This was followed by a synthesis of limitations and field-specific gaps. Cross-field analysis revealed only four papers demonstrating overlap within the reviewed corpus: three showing implicit connections between HCD and HRI, and one showing implicit overlap between BID and HRI with indirect ties to HCD. This review lays the groundwork for more integrated design research by identifying opportunities for collaboration across BID, HCD, and HRI, highlighting the potential for more biologically-informed, user-centered, and socially responsive robotic systems.

candidates.title: The impact of encouraging utterances by a human partner and a conversational robot on older adults’ subjective well-being: a 6-week sustained interaction
candidates.abstract: Introduction In human–human communication, encouragement has been closely associated with subjective well-being (SWB). However, the long-term effects of encouragement in human–robot interaction remain unclear, particularly in comparison with human-delivered encouragement and across different encouragement strategy types. SWB comprises both affective well-being (AWB) and cognitive well-being (CWB). This study investigated whether sustained verbal encouragement from a human partner and a conversational robot could enhance older adults’ SWB. Methods A two-phase design was adopted. First, a preliminary online survey with 55 older Japanese adults (aged 65–74) was conducted to select encouragement strategies for the main experiment, identifying offering specific actions (high-efficacy) and distraction (low-efficacy) as two encouragement strategies that differed significantly in participants’ perceived effectiveness (p < 0.05). Based on this survey, 18 older Japanese adults (aged 62–90) were recruited for an exploratory 6-week longitudinal experiment. Participants interacted with either a human partner or a conversational robot once per week and were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: human partner or social robot (RoBoHoN) crossed with high- or low-perceived-efficacy encouragement strategy. SWB was assessed using questionnaires, while post-session open-ended responses, diary entries, and post-experiment interviews provided qualitative data on encouragement experience, perceived SWB changes, and participants’ perceived sources of SWB change. Results Results suggested that high-efficacy verbal encouragement may positively influence older adults’ SWB, possibly with a stronger effect than low-efficacy encouragement, with a crossover-like pattern emerging: for AWB, the advantage of high-efficacy over low-efficacy encouragement tended to be more pronounced in the robot condition (Δ gap = 2.8) than the human condition (Δ gap = 0.5), whereas for CWB, it appeared to be more pronounced in the human condition (Δ gap = 2.0) than the robot condition (Δ gap = 0.2); these crossover trends should be interpreted with caution given the small sample size. Qualitative findings further suggested that the conversation itself may have contributed to participants’ perceived emotional support in the Japanese cultural context. Discussion These preliminary longitudinal findings suggest that social robots and human partners may both contribute to supporting older adults’ SWB and may play complementary roles.

candidates.title: Human–Robot Interaction and Ergonomics
candidates.abstract: Robots in the workplace are becoming a familiar sight. Hence, they have become the focus of debates and research on workplace ergonomics. While this emerging technology holds great promise to improve environments, this can only be achieved through the intentional application of ergonomic principles. Physical, cognitive and organizational ergonomics must be considered when talking about human-robot interaction (HRI) in a work environment. This chapter presents fundamentals on both human-robot interaction and ergonomics. This includes key topics such as potential roles of humans in HRI, interaction design and interfaces. Furthermore, it presents key domains of HRI and the emerging perspectives in research and application. It underscores the importance of an interdisciplinary approach in assessing the impact of robotics on humans and emphasizes the need for a human-centered design philosophy when developing innovative robotic systems.

candidates.title: Why overtrust in social robots is inevitable
candidates.abstract: Abstract When robots enter our social spaces, we may view them from three different perspectives: as machines, as artefacts with specific affordances (like ‘seeing’, ‘speaking’, ‘dancing’), or as nonstandard characters, which people construct based on the features of the robot depicted, the way it is framed by others, and influenced by their own needs and dispositions. People can switch seamlessly between the three perspectives, for example, offering polite assistance in one minute and turning it off for cleaning in the next. However, when robots are construed as characters, they become social actors, and with this sociality, also expectations concerning trust apply. The fact that they participate in activities that rest on human social interaction mechanisms is likely to lead to overtrust in these characters since it evokes general pragmatic principles, like recipient design, grounding and drawing on common ground. In this paper, I present experimental evidence that it is possible to block overtrust to some extent, but that regulating people’s trust in social robots remains challenging.

candidates.title: HFE Considerations in Sustainability in Robotics
candidates.abstract: Sustainability can be conceptualized as three interlinked aspects: economic; social; and natural capital. In this chapter we will examine what is required for each of these aspects from a human factors and ergonomics perspective to enable sustainability in human-robotic systems. When looking at the economic and social capital nexus it is important to take into account issues of safety and the future roles of humans in robotic systems. This includes issues such as skills, training, resilience, and employment status of the humans. Furthermore, the possibilities arising from advanced social robotics also requires an examination of issues such as privacy, trust, and understandability. When looking at the economic and natural capital nexus it is necessary to consider aspects such as the materials used to produce, maintain, and deconstruct robotic systems as well as the eco-efficiencies and eco-effectiveness that can be obtained from including robotics in human systems. Such an examination requires a consideration of the diverse impact of robotic systems in different geographical communities, and among regions with different economic development status. The social and natural capital nexus requires us to evaluate when and where to invest in human-robotic systems, but also when and where to resist such developments. Finally, we consider the HFE values that are needed to help develop a more sustainable approach to the development of human-robotic systems.

candidates.title: LLM-Based Waypoint Authoring via Augmented Reality for Human–Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Augmented reality (AR) can make robot programming more intuitive by letting users set motion parameters directly in the workspace. This paper extends AURaPath, an AR system for interactive 6-DoF waypoint determination on a UR10 collaborative robot using HoloLens2, with a voice modality for hands-free authoring. The voice layer follows a two-tier design: an on-device keyword recognizer handles the safety-critical verbs behind a two-step confirmation gate, and a large language model (LLM) maps the resulting transcript to the system’s structured command set so that operators need not memorize fixed phrases; the deployed pipeline takes spoken microphone input, while the benchmark below evaluates the transcript-to-command mapping stage in isolation. We evaluate the mapping layer on an objective benchmark of 169 labeled utterances that isolates language-to-command mapping from speech recognition and robot execution, and we compare a deterministic keyword baseline, four local models on a single consumer GPU, and free-tier cloud backends. The keyword baseline cannot express parameterized authoring commands and scores zero on every authoring field, while a free-tier cloud model reaches 95.3% exact-match results, averaged over 10 runs. The reject analysis shows that the ability to decline out-of-scope input, rather than raw accuracy, determines whether a model is suitable for the language-mapping tier of our safety-gated architecture, in which a deterministic layer and a preview-before-execute gate remain responsible for execution, which supports keeping the safety-critical verbs on the deterministic layer. The benchmark selects the backend that the deployed system uses, on the same physical UR10 demonstrated in the base system. The project code, the evaluation harness and dataset, and the base-system demonstration are available on GitHub (Please see Data Availability Statement section).

candidates.title: User Experiences With a Social Robot for Cardiometabolic Risk Assessment in a Community Setting in Uppsala, Sweden: Qualitative Semistructured Interview Study
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background Cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs) are a major health concern worldwide, with people living in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas being disproportionately affected. Knowing one’s risk status for developing a CMD can help individuals in delaying or preventing the disease. Innovative tools and strategies such as the use of AI-based technology are needed to improve inclusivity, cost-effectiveness, and sustainability of screening processes. Objective This study aimed to assess users’ perceptions of the usability and acceptance of the social robot “Furhat” for cardiometabolic risk assessment within a socioeconomically disadvantaged community in Uppsala, Sweden. Methods In this qualitative study, 13 semistructured interviews were conducted with participants living in socially disadvantaged areas within Uppsala, after they completed a CMD risk assessment delivered by the social robot. The study was conducted in one of the socioeconomically disadvantaged areas in Uppsala from October 19 to 26, 2023. Participants were purposefully sampled at different community events via phone or on the street to achieve the desired variation regarding personal characteristics such as age, gender, or area of living. The used interview guide for this study consisted of questions regarding the demographics, participants’ experiences with the robot screening, and suggestions for improvements. A framework analysis approach was applied to the data. Results Two themes were developed. The first theme Self-versus-others: a matter of perception, norms, and assumptions includes participants’ perceptions of who would use the robot and why, if it was installed in the community. Participants perceived older individuals, immigrants, and, in some instances, women to be less interested in the robot screening or as having a harder time participating in it. However, there were between-group variations, especially among men and women, with participants often discounting opinions ascribed to their group by others. The second theme The robot is good, but humans are better captures participants’ actual experiences of the interaction with the social robot once they have started the interaction. Although participants enjoyed the interaction with the robot, perceived it as nonjudgmental, and would recommend it to others, most would prefer conducting the screening with a human. Two major contributors for this preference were language barriers experienced during the robot-participant interaction, as well as their wish for more interactive, emotionally responsive, and communicative features of the robot. Conclusions This study provides insights into users’ perceptions of the usability and acceptance of a social robot for risk assessment in a community context, which can help inform the further development of this technology for health screening in a community context. In the future, the robot could be further developed to conduct risk assessments in multiple languages and offer a broader service to users, such as providing appropriate information related to healthy and active living.

candidates.title: The emerging charisma of 0 s and 1s: unraveling the intricacies of virtual idol adoption
candidates.abstract: Abstract This research explores the factors that influence perception, adoption intention, and trust of K-pop virtual idols. Drawing on a unified stimulus-organism-response (S–O-R) framework integrated with parasocial interaction (PSI) theory, this study investigates how industry-driven environmental stimuli (i.e., visual appeal, narrative openness, socially present conversational style, content-driven engagement, institutional trust) shape the internal psychological state of the audience to drive adoption behavior. The study employs an online survey of K-pop fans ( N = 259) with a series of statistical analyses to examine the relationships between the identified factors and outcome variables. The results demonstrate that relational and identity-driven stimuli operate as dominant predictors that effectively bridge the psychological distance caused by the idol's artificial nature. In contrast, visual appeal and institutional trust exhibit critical boundary limitations. Crucially, the findings reveal that realistic perception and parasocial relationship serve as the underlying mechanisms that translate digital stimuli into genuine emotional trust and long-term behavioral commitment. This study contributes to the emerging field of virtual idol research, providing implications for virtual idol creators, developers, and industry stakeholders seeking to enhance adoption rates and fan engagement.

candidates.title: A study on user continuance intention for children’s intelligent companion robots based on BERTopic-PLS-SEM-fsQCA
candidates.abstract: The children’s intelligent companion robot market faces the industry-wide challenge of “high initial adoption yet low sustained retention.” Existing research has predominantly relied on single-method approaches, leaving the psychological mechanisms and configurational pathways driving user continuance intention insufficiently understood. This study constructs a sequential multi-method research framework integrating “BERTopic thematic mining—PLS-SEM linear validation—fsQCA configurational analysis.” Drawing on 6,405 valid online reviews from JD.com and 440 valid questionnaire responses, the study adopts an integrated theoretical framework combining the Expectation Confirmation Model (ECM) and the Value-based Adoption Model (VAM). BERTopic thematic mining identified six core demand dimensions from consumer reviews: perceived usefulness, perceived enjoyment, visual aesthetics, social/gifting value, technical reliability, and expectation confirmation. PLS-SEM analysis reveals that satisfaction is the strongest predictor of continuance intention ( β = 0.705, p < 0.001), explaining 50.3% of its variance ( R ² = 0.503). Perceived value ( R ² = 0.571) is jointly driven by expectation confirmation ( β = 0.230), perceived usefulness ( β = 0.197), technical reliability ( β = 0.163), social/gifting value ( β = 0.141), visual aesthetics ( β = 0.106), and perceived enjoyment ( β = 0.104). Notably, perceived enjoyment exhibits a distinctive dual-pathway mechanism, influencing continuance intention both indirectly through perceived value and directly through satisfaction ( β = 0.232, p < 0.001). Further fsQCA configuration analysis identified four configurations of high continuance intention (with a solution consistency rate of 0.811 and a coverage rate of 0.469), which can be grouped into three broader patterns based on their theoretical coherence: the “expectation confirmation-dominated” pattern (Configurations 1 and 2, with consistency rates of 0.855 and 0.839, respectively), the “full-dimensional attribute-driven” pattern (Configuration 3, consistency rate of 0.814), and the “Social-Hedonic Compensation” pattern (Configuration 4, consistency rate of 0.836), indicating substantial heterogeneity in continuance intention logic across different segments. Theoretically, this study extends the ECM-VAM framework to the context of children’s embodied intelligent products by introducing visual aesthetics and technical reliability as context-specific antecedents of perceived value, demonstrates that unstructured online review texts can serve as a valid source for the contextualized operationalization of theoretical constructs, and qualifies the linear assumptions of conventional net-effect models through a configurational perspective.

candidates.title: Designing robot-to-robot interaction to support early-stage engagement in a teleoperated Robot Avatar system with multiple robots
candidates.abstract: Teleoperated Robot Avatars enable operators to provide customer service from remote locations. Effective persuasive interaction requires more than information presentation; customers' attention and engagement must be elicited before their attitudes and behavior can be influenced. Social presence may support this type of engagement. Based on prior research, we conceptualize a Robot Avatar's social presence as the extent to which customers perceive it, i.e., not as a machine or information medium, but as a social entity customers can attend to and interact with. Therefore, we examined a design approach intended to enhance a Robot Avatar's social presence by forming a social context around it. We developed GayaRobo, comprising one teleoperated Robot Avatar and two supporting Gaya robots. Rather than approaching users as independent agents, the Gaya robots respond to the Robot Avatar's utterances via speech and movement, thereby forming a social context centered on the avatar. We conducted a field experiment at a commercial complex in Osaka, Japan, to compare observable early-stage engagement behaviors of passersby toward the Robot Avatar across three experimental conditions. The same three-robot configuration was used under three conditions: the Gaya robots responded to the Robot Avatar, only the Robot Avatar spoke, or only the Gaya robots spoke. Two annotators coded four behaviors among 1,379 passersby in 270 min of video recordings: looking at the Robot Avatar, approaching it, talking to it, and picking up a flyer. After correction for multiple testing, only approaching the Robot Avatar was significantly associated with experimental condition and occurred more frequently than expected under the inter-robot interaction condition. These findings provide behavioral evidence that the inter-robot interaction condition was associated with approaching the Robot Avatar, an observable indicator of early-stage engagement. Because social presence was not directly measured, the findings did not demonstrate that GayaRobo enhanced the Robot Avatar's social presence. Nevertheless, they highlight approach behavior as a relevant observable outcome for future evaluations of designs that consider the social context surrounding a Robot Avatar in customer service settings.

candidates.title: Human–Robot Interaction in Industrial Contexts
candidates.abstract: Technological advances in industrial robotics have significantly changed modern working environments, enabling greater autonomy, flexibility and productivity. Here the emergence of advanced robots designed for direct interaction with humans play a substantial role. By integrating emerging technologies such as AI, machine learning, and sophisticated interaction design, advanced robots are reshaping industries. All while increasing efficiency and customization and remaining cost-effective. Despite their benefits, the use of robotic systems also brings challenges, particularly in the area of occupational safety and health. After an overview of the evolution of different robotic systems, a description of industrial work tasks, related working conditions and highlighted risk and opportunities associated with automation, this chapter examines key safety factors that are essential for close human–robot interaction and assesses their impact on workers. Two case studies illustrate how the practical application of advanced robotic systems in industrial settings affects workplace dynamics. The chapter further highlights the role of worker expectations and experience in relation to advanced robotics. By combining empirical evidence with real-world applications, this chapter underscores the importance of adaptable, user-friendly robotic systems that prioritize worker well-being alongside operational efficiency. In doing so, it contributes to the broader dialogue on sustainable, ergonomic innovation in the workplace and highlights the critical role of human-centered design in the future of industrial robotics.

candidates.title: E-skin for human–robot interaction: tactile sensing and edge computing architectures
candidates.abstract: Electronic skin (E-skin) has been a key enabling technology for robots that need to work safely, intelligently, and in physical proximity with humans. The domain has progressed from fingertip tactile arrays to large-area, full-body systems that can now sense pressure, shear, high-frequency vibration, proximity (i.e., the distinct sensation of “touching” another body), temperature, and even social touch. In this article, we showcase the architectural bottlenecks, material science challenges, and embedded computing requirements that influence whether E-skin can transition from laboratory prototypes to deployable robotic systems. From our analysis, we showcase that none of the currently available transduction principles satisfy all requirements of spatial resolution, conformability, low latency, low cost, calibration stability, and mechanical robustness. Capacitive and time-of-flight methods improve pre-touch awareness, pneumatic and barometric schemes enhance coverage and low cost, and tomographic approaches and row–column strategies reduce wiring, while deep learning techniques enable semantic recognition of human tactile gestures. Simultaneously, this paper claims that the next E-skin trends will be built on top of heterogeneous architectures composed of soft materials, distributed sensor nodes, deterministic safety loops, and edge computing platforms based on Arduino, Raspberry Pi, Onion Omega, and NVIDIA Jetson devices alike. Lastly, two comparative tables and a scoping process informed by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) were used to clarify the evidence base and technological trade-offs.

candidates.title: Rapport-building dialogue strategy: a comprehensive analysis of human subjective, behavioral and facial emotional engagement
candidates.abstract: Purpose Rapport is a conversational aspect focused on relationship building. Because rapport can influence outcomes in collaborative tasks, this study proposes a concrete methodology for introducing rapport-building into dialogue systems, namely a rapport-building dialogue strategy, and evaluates its effectiveness. Design/methodology/approach We implemented a rapport-building dialogue strategy for virtual agents by prompting a large language model (LLM) based on psychological theories of rapport. We employed two dialogue approaches, a predefined sequence and a free-form approach, to guide dialogue generation and compared their performance through human evaluations. To analyze the human aspects of rapport further, we conducted subjective, behavioral and facial emotion assessments. Findings Our experimental results show that the system based on a free-form dialogue strategy, which allows the adaptive use of rapport-building strategies, achieves the highest subjective scores. Our human-centered analyses reveal strong associations between rapport perception and user experience, indicating that perceived rapport is closely aligned with engagement and experiential quality. We observe directional tendencies in behavioral and emotional patterns, with more expressive participants tending to report higher rapport scores, suggesting potential associations that warrant further investigation. Research limitations/implications While these findings provide valuable insights, the study's scope was limited to 20 Japanese graduate students; future work could benefit from extending this study with larger participant samples and cross-cultural investigations. Originality/value This study introduces: (1) a rapport-building dialogue strategy; and (2) a comprehensive analysis that distinguishes statistically-supported drivers of rapport from promising signals and non-influential factors. Together, they offer structured guidance for the development and evaluation of future rapport-building dialogue systems.

candidates.title: Do Visual Features Improve Other-Initiated Repair Detection? A Dyadic Multimodal Approach
candidates.abstract: Other-initiated Self-repair, or in short Other-initiated Repair (OIR), is an essential mechanism in conversational interaction, whereby a recipient signals a problem in speaking, hearing, or understanding, prompting the previous speaker to resolve it. In the case of conversational agents, it is essential to accurately identify these repair initiation strategies to address communication breakdowns efficiently. While conversational analysis studies have shown that OIR initiation is accompanied by both verbal and non-verbal signals such as gaze shifts, facial expressions, body postures, and hand gestures, existing computational approaches rely mainly on text and audio. This paper introduces a novel multimodal model for OIR detection and classification, incorporating a set of visual features drawn from conversation analysis. We evaluate our approach on two corpora with distinct languages and interaction settings. Results demonstrate that visual information consistently improves performance over text and audio baselines, and provide insights into cross-modal feature contributions across two corpora.

candidates.title: Trust in Human-Chatbot Interaction: An Integrated Model of Performance Expectancy and Decision Making
candidates.abstract: The communicative behaviour of users has changed with the evolution and advancements of technology, significantly altering the dynamics of human machine interactions.The rapid integration of chatbots into everyday life, particularly in healthcare, has intensified the need to understand the role of trust in human–computer interaction. While existing models of technology adoption—such as the UnifiedTheory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)—emphasize performance expectancy and ease of use, they often overlook the socio-psychological construct of trust that shapes users' willingness to depend on conversational agents. This study integrates UTAUT, TAM, and the Human–Computer Trust Model (HCTM) to examine how trust influences performance expectancy and decision-making in human–chatbot communication.A web-based survey of 255 users aged 18–45 in South Asia was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results demonstrate that trust has a strong and direct positive effect on both performance expectancy and decision-making. Model evaluation indicated robust predictive power (R² values above 0.89) and acceptable fit indices (SRMR = 0.042, NFI = 0.929). These findings highlight trust as a central determinant in chatbot adoption, shifting the discourse from purely functional acceptance to relational and affective dynamics.By empirically validating trust as a key predictor of technology use outcomes, this study extends current acceptance models and provides actionable insights for the design of reliable, transparent, and ethically responsible chatbots. The findings have particular relevance for healthcare and other high-stakes domains, where user trust is indispensable for effective decision support and engagement

candidates.title: Estimating the Causal Impact of Social Navigation Signals in Corridor Scenarios
candidates.abstract: Deploying robots in human-shared environments requires deciding not only how to navigate, but also when dedicated social signals are worth emitting. Classic observation-based inference can be misleading in such settings: confounding factors may bias the estimated relationship between a signal and the task outcome, leading to incorrect decisions. Causal inference provides a framework for disentangling these relationships by modelling the mechanisms linking observations, actions, and outcomes, and by estimating interventional effects after accounting for confounding paths. We study a human-robot interaction scenario in a corridor and use a causal model to estimate whether a social navigation signal causally improves transit success. We represent the interaction as a causal DAG involving robot action, pedestrian occupancy, available space, task outcome, and a controlled confounder (static obstacles). We compare the interventional estimate with the observational estimate obtained by conditioning only on the robot action, which does not explicitly model interventions. Our results show that accounting for confounding variables can reverse the conclusions drawn from naive observational analysis: the observational estimate wrongly suggests that the social signal is detrimental, whereas the causal estimate shows that it is beneficial. This discrepancy highlights how failing to account for confounding can lead to incorrect conclusions and demonstrates the importance of causal models for context-aware signalling decisions in social robot navigation.

candidates.title: “Cute Companion” or “Awful Thing”: Understanding individual differences in attitudes to social robots as pets
Digital Human Modeling in Human–Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: In human–robot collaboration, there are different levels of interaction. At lower levels, collisions must be avoided. At a higher level, collaborative robots directly interact with humans, and human health and safety need to be assured when designing work systems with robots included. In the process, adequate models of human motions are required. The diversity of human motions has led to ongoing research activities that have provided a considerable range of models. This chapter provides an overview of full-body human models such as kinematics, dynamics, and skin models and their applications in robotics. Kinematic models provide an abstraction of the human skeleton structure and its joints, whereas skin models provide mappings from the skeleton models to skin surfaces. Both are required for motion simulation with most human motion models. A survey of analytical, physics and data-driven human motion models is given. The state of the art as well as recent research advances are summarized for the models, and models of singular human motions and motion corridor/density models are differentiated. Their relevance for different levels of human–robot collaboration and ergonomics is discussed. Applications of motion models in the collaborative robotics domain and their respective advantages and shortcomings are reviewed with a special focus on their applicability for safety, efficiency and user experience in digital twins. Finally, the chapter presents three application scenarios in assembly lines and material handling in automotive industry.

candidates.title: Quantifying the Subjective Experience in Human–Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Assessing the quality of interaction between collaborative robots (i.e., cobots) and humans to achieve a (shared) goal is an essential part of supporting the diffusion of usable and safe collaborative robotic systems. The key issue here is that cobots within and between domains can vary substantially in terms of features even when these are meant to support similar tasks. Under this perspective, it seems very hard, if not impossible, to identify coherent ways to benchmark the quality of cobots. However, all the cobots share one element which is that they have to deal with humans and satisfy them. This chapter claims that focusing on how a system can satisfy the human counterpart can (indirectly) provide insights into the quality of cobots that can be a piece of valuable information for the designers. In this sense, identifying and validating a set of key aspects to assess the subjective experience in interaction with robots during collaborative tasks is a stepping stone for benchmarking cobots. We will discuss how, in other domains, researchers developed standardized scales to ensure comparable results regarding the user experience (UX), and to model the differences between systems. Moreover, based on a recent systematic literature review, an initial list of key aspects to evaluate UX with cobots is discussed as a step to build and validate a future tool for unifying how experts evaluate cobots.

candidates.title: Mapping older adults´ use of social robots: An institutional ethnographic perspective
candidates.abstract: Technology has been seen as a solution to the challenges related to the care of older adults, and it is possible to talk about “the ageing-and-innovation discourse” (Neven & Peine, 2017). This study used institutional ethnography to explore the presence of the discourse in a care home in Finland. A map of the discourse was produced from the viewpoint of older adults who participated in robot workshops, by interacting with the robots and discussing about them, in the care home. The analysis of Finnish policy documents revealed an overarching discourse on aging and innovation, in which technology was linked to economic growth, public sector efficiency, and improved access to care. The participants placed themselves on the map as learners, users and innovators of technology. The researchers were viewed as sources of information, care workers as enablers of robot use and engineers as designers of robots. The robots were viewed as having instrumental value and as objects to be utilised.

candidates.title: Potential and limitations of socially assistive robots to support malnutrition care: a critical reflection by dietitians
candidates.abstract: Nutrition is essential for the physical and psychological well-being and health of older adults. Malnutrition negatively affects both their physical and mental health and their overall quality of life. Dietitians face challenges in supporting older adults due to time constraints, which can limit the continuity of care. While previous research highlights the potential of assistive technologies to help reduce malnutrition, such as socially assistive robots (SARs), these approaches lack a holistic perspective and insufficiently address collaborative processes within the broader care network. This study presents the findings from a Research-through-Design (RtD) study in which eight dietitians from four practices participated in context-mapping sessions involving personas, generative design probes, ranking exercises, and speculative design activities to critically reflect on the potential role of socially assistive robots in supporting collaborative malnutrition care. The results were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. These results highlight key challenges in nutritional care, including the social nature of eating, the need for personalized support, and challenges within the care network. These findings informed potential roles for SARs, including reinforcing dietary advice, supporting shared decision-making, facilitating collaboration, and encouraging shared eating moments. Crucially, the findings suggest that the value of SARs depends less on adding new functionalities than on carefully positioning their role within collaborative nutritional care. This includes preserving older adults’ autonomy, clearly allocating responsibilities between dietitians and technology, supporting meaningful engagement between consultations, and maintaining appropriate professional boundaries.

candidates.title: Mutual Adaptation and Influence: Review of Latent Dynamics Models in Human–Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in robotics have enabled more dynamic and interactive roles when working with humans. This progress is enabled in part by latent state models, which allow the robot to predict human actions in a compact and tractable way. This paradigm has allowed robots not only to respond and adapt to human behavior but also to anticipate and plan proactively through the use of latent dynamics models. This review explores the use of such models in the field of human–robot interaction. Existing literature reveals three classes of latent dynamics models: Bayesian, Markovian, and encoded. To connect these works, we synthesize a unified framework consisting of a prediction and control step. This framework shows how the traditional one‐way adaptation extends to mutually adaptive behaviors by using latent dynamics in the prediction step. Similarly, we show how influence is an extension of mutual adaptation by using latent dynamics in the control step. We then review state‐of‐the‐art approaches to mutual adaptation and influence for the three latent dynamics classes and discuss emergent properties as they relate to application, update frequency, and specific considerations for mutual adaptation or influence. Using this review, we highlight gaps in the current literature and propose future directions.

candidates.title: How metaverse influencers shape electronic word-of-mouth: Credibility, attractiveness, and parasocial relationships across cultures and gender
candidates.abstract: Metaverse Influencers (MVIs) are technologically constructed social actors increasingly promoting tourism destinations. However, they continue to be viewed as uncannily or authentically fake, raising questions about whether followers perceive them as credible, form meaningful parasocial relationships with them, and intend to recommend the destinations they endorse. To address these gaps, this study integrated source credibility theory, parasocial relationship theory, and the similarity-attractiveness model and tested a framework linking source credibility and physical attractiveness to e-WOM intentions, with parasocial relationship as the mediator. Using a quantitative design across three cases (main effects/mediation; UK–USA–India; female–male), results showed that parasocial relationships increased e-WOM, and source credibility increased both parasocial relationships and e-WOM. Physical attractiveness did not directly increase e-WOM, but strengthened parasocial relationships, which fully mediated the attractiveness–e-WOM link; mediation was partial for credibility. Only one cross-country difference emerged (attractiveness to e-WOM was stronger in the USA), and one gender difference (attractiveness to parasocial relationship stronger for males). These findings show that the extent to which MVIs influence their followers is not only dependent upon the designed appearance of the MVI itself but also on whether followers perceive them as credible and develop parasocial relationships with them. The study enhances our knowledge of human relationships with synthetic social actors and provides insights into how MVIs should be created to responsibly promote tourism communications.
