candidates.title: A Multimodal Cross-Attention Framework for Robot Error Detection from Bystander Reactions
candidates.abstract: To detect human-robot interaction errors, existing approaches have primarily focused on behavioural responses from individuals directly involved in the interaction, whereas reactions from external observers have received comparatively little attention. Similarly, these approaches have been limited to interactions in controlled environments with little variability in lighting, camera angles, and background noise. Addressing these gaps, the ERR@HRI 3.0 challenge focuses on bystander error detection in unconstrained, real-world environments. Our primary submission is a time-aware multimodal fusion framework that combines facial and acoustic representations via bidirectional cross-attention. Two versions of this framework, with different encoding approaches, are evaluated against a bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) classifier with simple concatenation. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this cross-fusion approach for capturing errors and generalising to unseen real-world data. Our cross-fusion and BiLSTM models achieved the top-three positions on Track 1, outperforming the challenge baseline and other competing submissions. Feature importance analysis further revealed that smile-related action units and their temporal dynamics serve as primary discriminative cues for error detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/chardiwall/SHEF-HRI.

candidates.title: Understanding Older Adults’ And Caretakers’ Attitudes Toward Social Robots Using Natural Language Processing and Thematic Analysis
candidates.abstract: Abstract The present study aims to examine the role of social robots in enriching older adults’ environments and helping them cope with the problems that decrease their well-being and life quality. To understand how social robots can be integrated into older adults’ lives, we investigated both older adults’ and caretakers’ attitudes toward social robots. For this aim, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 30 participants. In these interviews, we showed them photos and videos of the three social robots with different looks, abilities, and degrees of resemblance to humans. Then, we asked them to answer some open-ended questions. These robots were the pet-like robot Aibo, the toy-like robot Paro, and the humanoid robot Pepper. We analyzed the answers using complementary quantitative and qualitative approaches. The quantitative approach included the Sentiment Analysis (SA) and the qualitative approach included the Thematic Analysis (TA). SA results indicate that caretakers approached negatively to Paro, and positively to Aibo and Pepper. On the other hand, older adults did not differ in the polarity of attitudes toward the three robots. The TA results yielded four overarching themes: I) Perceived and expected roles of the robot, II) Physical characteristics and design features of the robot, III) Factors influencing acceptance of the robot, and IV) Disadvantages of the robot. Under those, there were various themes and sub-themes diversified for each robot. Overall, our findings reveal significant insights into older adults’ and caretakers’ approaches to different types of social robots and enable researchers to use these robots more effectively.

candidates.title: A Humanoid Companion Robot in Residential Memory Care: Staff Perspectives During Early Implementation
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To examine memory support staff perspectives during early integration of a humanoid companion robot in a residential memory care neighborhood. METHOD: A qualitative descriptive design was used in a memory care neighborhood in Northern California. Data were collected from 15 staff participants through one pre-implementation focus group and three follow-up individual interviews. Interviews were conducted before and during the first 8 weeks of the robot's introduction and were audio recorded and transcribed verbatim. Six interdisciplinary team members performed thematic analysis through collaborative coding and team-based comparisons. RESULTS: . Staff reported varied readiness, recognized promise and limitations, and emphasized the need for staff as ongoing intermediaries between the robot and residents during use. CONCLUSION: Humanoid companion robots may support social engagement in memory care; however, effective implementation requires staff preparation, technological refinement, and alignment with person-centered care.

candidates.title: SHARE: Towards Head-Mounted AR with User-Centric SLAM in Shared Human-Robot Workspaces
candidates.abstract: Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) in shared physical spaces using Augmented Reality (AR) interfaces is powered by Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). Existing multi-agent SLAM systems rely on an edge server to combine visual findings of multiple resource-constrained agents, perform computation, and schedule updates to their local maps. However, the edge treats all agents uniformly and ignores the fundamentally different latency requirements of heterogeneous HRC agents: robots and head-mounted AR users. This uniform resource allocation often results in high lag for user manipulation, as it does not meet the stringent latency requirements of AR. In this work, we design, implement, and evaluate SHARE, a user-centric SLAM system that strategically prioritizes AR user experience while maintaining accurate tracking performance for robots. SHARE builds a first-of-its-kind experience model for HRC agents and adaptively adjusts transmission priorities to match it. To reduce end-to-end latency, SHARE leverages the redundancy of visual features acquired by agents in shared human-robot workspaces to reduce computation time induced by edge-based processing. Real-world deployment with commercial AR headsets and a ground robot achieves 13.22 ms average latency for AR users (43.3% reduction from baseline) while maintaining sub-2-centimeter tracking accuracy. User studies further reveal statistically significant improvements in user perception.

candidates.title: Toward intelligent safety assurance in construction human-robot collaboration
candidates.abstract: Construction human-robot collaboration (HRC) introduces physical, ergonomic, and cognitive risks that conventional isolated-based safeguards cannot adequately manage in dynamic, unstructured worksites and requires more adaptive forms of safety assurance. Although diverse robotics-related approaches have been developed, how they function as interconnected, active safety-assurance mechanisms for construction HRC remains insufficiently synthesised. This paper systematically reviews 215 studies published from 2011 to 2025 through PRISMA-guided screening, bibliometric analysis and thematic synthesis. Five connected technological directions are identified: robot design optimisation, context-aware perception, human-centric understanding and forecasting, autonomous robotic adaptation, and safety management. The synthesis shows a transition from passive risk avoidance toward perception-driven, prediction, and adaptive safety assurance, but 54% of studies remain limited to controlled laboratory validation, and few integrate uncertainty across sensing, prediction, control and supervision. Accordingly, a closed-loop framework is proposed to guide the integration and construction-realistic validation of verifiable, uncertainty-aware HRC safety systems.

candidates.title: Videogame spectatorship and orbital fandom value
candidates.abstract: This thesis examines the layered and evolving nature of online videogame fandoms, with a particular focus on what it terms orbital fandom; fan communities that emerged one or more step removed from the original game text. Rather than engaging directly with the game itself, these fans form attachment through derivative content, content creators, and platform-medicated interactions. By shifting attention to these decentralised forms of engagement, the thesis expands existing models of fandom to account for the complex social, affective, and economic dynamics that shape participation in contemporary digital game cultures. To explore these dynamics, the research draws on a mixed-methods approach combining virtual ethnography, semi-structured stakeholder interviews, and a participant journaling study. This methodology allows for both creator- and viewer-centred perspectives, capturing how value; cultural, social, and monetary is produced, circulated, and contested within platformed fan ecosystems. The thesis develops the Orbital Fandom Framework, a conceptual model that articulates how these forms of fandom operate within the wider infrastructures of platform governance and digital labour. Empirical findings reveal how fan labour often takes place under informal, precarious, and frequently unacknowledged conditions. At the same time, fan contributions, particularly within orbital fandoms, play a vital role in shaping visibility, community cohesion, and even commercial success within the games industry. The thesis also explores the emotional intensities of parasocial relationships and the ethical concerns surrounding platform incentives and exploitation. These findings hold relevance not only for academic debates in game and fan studies but also for developers and platform designers seeking to engage with fan communities in more ethical and inclusive ways. By introducing a new conceptual vocabulary, advancing a critical framework, and offering practical insights, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the socio-cultural and economic life of videogame fandoms in the platform era.

candidates.title: Hardware implementation of AI-based fuzzy logic for real-time sign language interpreter robotic control using FPGA
candidates.abstract: Abstract Communication barriers between hearing-impaired individuals and non-sign language users remain a significant challenge in modern society. Existing sign language recognition systems primarily focus on unidirectional communication and are often limited by high latency, excessive power consumption, and lack of robustness in uncertain environments. This paper proposes a novel FPGA-based Bidirectional Robotic Sign Language Communication System (BRSLCS) integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI), fuzzy logic, and robotic control for real-time assistive communication. The proposed architecture supports both forward communication, where sign language gestures are translated into text or speech, and reverse communication, where text or speech is converted into robotic sign language gestures through an actuated robotic hand. In the forward communication flow, gesture images captured using a camera are processed through preprocessing, feature extraction, AI-based classification, and fuzzy inference stages. In the reverse communication flow, speech or textual inputs are interpreted using Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques and mapped into robotic sign gestures controlled using FPGA-based actuation logic. The integration of fuzzy logic improves classification robustness and interpretability under uncertain conditions such as illumination variation, gesture ambiguity, and motion blur. FPGA implementation provides deterministic timing, low latency, hardware parallelism, and energy efficiency suitable for embedded real-time systems. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed system achieves 92-95% recognition accuracy with latency between 10-25 ms while consuming only 4-6 W power, outperforming conventional CPU and GPU-based implementations. The proposed BRSLCS provides a scalable and practical framework for inclusive communication systems in healthcare, education, public services, and human-robot interaction environments.

candidates.title: Robotic Pet or Soft Toy? An Autoethnographic Study of Living with MetaCat in the Home
candidates.abstract: Lifelike robotic cats, covered in soft fur and sensor-embedded, are now commercially available and being targeted at home settings. Typically, they are designed to respond to human touch and voice with pet-like behaviours such as purring, meowing and tail wagging. This ambivalence between pet-like form and robotic features raises questions about how they will integrate into home life. Will family members treat them like pets, toys or something else? Research has focused on their use for health and aged care but less so on everyday use in families. We conducted an autoethnography combined with observations in which nine researcher-participants with diverse backgrounds, ages and life settings spent up to ten days each with a robot cat called MetaCat. Our findings elicited surprising, sometimes contradictory experiences and feelings. We report on where MetaCat was placed in the home and the interactions it triggered. We discuss benefits, tensions and design implications when developing pet-like versus robot-like products.

candidates.title: Message Over Modality: Toward a Source-Agnostic Message Evaluation Framework for AI-Delivered Social Support
candidates.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly take on socially supportive roles, questions remain about how users perceive such support across different AI modalities (i.e., the form through which an AI system communicates, such as voice, embodiment, or text). This study examines early-stage evaluations formed after a single initial interaction with three common AI modalities, voice-based assistants (VBAs), social robots, and text-based generative AI, delivering either informational or emotional support. Using a 3 (AI modality: VBA vs. social robot vs. text-based generative AI) × 2 (support type: emotional vs informational) between-subjects experimental design, participants (N = 203) viewed scripted video vignettes of human–AI encounters and then evaluated the AI agents on credibility (competence, character, caring), task and social attraction, and perceived support. Results revealed that all agents were rated significantly above the midpoint on most attributes, suggesting users accept AI agents as credible and supportive. However, no significant differences emerged between AI types. Instead, support type had a stronger influence; informational support increased perceived competence, while emotional support elevated perceptions of caring. Qualitative responses supported these trends, emphasizing message relevance over agent form. These findings introduce and support the Source-Agnostic Message Evaluation (SAME) framework, which proposes that in early-stage, observational AI support contexts, users assess AI support based more on what is said than who, or what, says it. This has implications for AI design, emphasizing message quality over modality in user experience optimization.

candidates.title: In View or Out of View? A Vision-Aware Filter that Infers and Reacts to the Human's Field of View
candidates.abstract: During human-robot interaction, sight plays an important role. When the human sees a robot, they can observe the robot's actions and better predict the robot's future behaviors. Conversely, when the human cannot see the robot, they become uncertain about the robot's intent and plans. In this paper, we focus on the human's field of view. Existing human-aware planners either ignore this field of view and assume the human can observe the entire scene, or intentionally design their interactions so the robot is always visible to the human. By contrast, we enable robots to infer what the human has and has not seen during interaction, i.e., the human's field of view. We then apply this estimate as a vision-aware filter on the robot's actions. Given a nominal robot policy and a model of the interaction, we roll out the policy over a short horizon to see how the robot's state updates. We then reweight the actions based on how those actions impact the robot's predicted visibility: higher weights are assigned to actions that bring the robot into (or away from) the human's line of sight. In practice, our framework provides an online estimation and filtering process that repeatedly updates its understanding of the human's field of view and then locally perturbs robot actions based on the human's vision. We evaluate our vision-aware filter on robots that assist humans in collaborative cooking and coordinate with them in driving environments. Across simulations and a 12-participant user study, we find that our vision-aware filter changes both performance and preference: participants completed over three times as many subtasks with in-view assistance while cooking, and had fewer collisions with cars that purposely stayed out of their view while driving.

candidates.title: Physical Ergonomics in Robotics
candidates.abstract: With the emergence of embodied intelligent systems like collaborative robots (cobots), the landscape of physically demanding work is changing. Indeed, robotic devices can augment human strength, optimize performance, and minimize the physical demands associated with a job or a task. These achievements of human-robot interaction (HRI) surely match the objectives of physical ergonomics: making physical interactions between humans and other elements of a system more efficient, more gratifying, and safer. One of the key goals of physical ergonomics certainly is to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs). Therefore, a cobot must have insight into the effect of physical stress on the human body. One of the most common ways to provide that is to use the established ergonomics look-up tables that indicate which working configurations and conditions may cause WMSDs based on experience. Another approach is to use musculoskeletal models to get real-time estimates of key internal body parameters, such as joint torques, muscle forces, and muscle fatigue. A cobotic or, in general, robotic system can then use these ergonomic indexes and variables to guide a human co-worker to more favourable configurations and conditions. In this chapter, we examine physical human-robot interactions (pHRIs) to have an introductory overview of possible scenarios and constraints. We then look into the fundamentals of physical ergonomics such as anthropometry, biomechanics, and environmental factors, including important ergonomic assessment tools and innovative indicators developed in robotics. Subsequently, concrete examples of methods that address physical ergonomics with collaborative robotics are examined in terms of design and control methods.

candidates.title: Ergonomics, Robotics, and Disciplinary Integration
candidates.abstract: Ergonomics is inherently based on disciplinary integration: a compulsory condition to lead the systemic understanding and improvement of real-world complexities like the ones of Human-Robot Interactions (HRIs). Accordingly, this chapter ponders the contributions of diverse disciplines to the study of human factors alongside their synergies with the multi-faceted area of robotics. Key examples are presented, considering problems requiring approaches like bio-inspired soft robotics, value-sensitive design, interactions and affective features, and neuroergonomics in HRI. The implications about education on HRI ergonomics are also pondered. Overall, this chapter remarks how diverse backgrounds can lead to contributions to the human-centered design and assessment of robots if the experts, regardless of disciplinary boundaries, just focus on learning novel perspectives and methods to solve the problems occurring in Human-Robot Systems.

candidates.title: Humans and Robots in Agriculture
candidates.abstract: Research in agricultural robotics has garnered increasing attention over the past decade. Simultaneously, Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) has emerged as a possible solution to increase automation and reduce the lack of human labor in the field. This chapter presents a study of research trends in HRI focusing on Artificial Intelligence (AI), human factors, and ergonomics in collaborative agricultural tasks. For example, we talk about the importance of robotics and the application of the different AI-based methods for HRI in field applications. Moreover, we emphasize situation awareness, stress, sleepiness, sleep quality, and distraction. We also explore various crucial and innovative topics related to HRI in agriculture, including safety, human factors, ergonomics, awareness, productivity, and management. This analysis shows that HRI paradigms can be effectively applied in agricultural applications, yielding promising production, safety, and farm management benefits, such as increasing productivity and reducing human workload.

candidates.title: Mixed emotions evoked when incongruent outward appearance and motion are combined
candidates.abstract: Understanding mixed emotions is crucial for capturing the ambivalence of human information processing. However, how specific visual factors, such as outward appearance and motion, interact to evoke these conflicting feelings remains unclear. Here, we present three-dimensional (3D) characters as visual stimuli that evoke mixed feelings, providing empirical insights into emotional phenomena such as “kimo-kawaii” by focusing on their outward appearances and motions. Congruent stimuli (e.g., pleasant appearance with pleasant motion) and incongruent stimuli (e.g., pleasant appearance with unpleasant motion) were evaluated. Characters with congruent features evoked a single feeling: pleasant or unpleasant. In contrast, the combination of pleasant outward appearance and unpleasant motion evoked both pleasant and unpleasant feelings. Moreover, the combination of unpleasant outward appearance and pleasant motion strongly evoked unpleasant feelings rather than pleasant feelings. These findings suggest that, within the present stimulus set, outward appearance may exert a stronger influence on affective evaluation than motion. The observed co-activation of positive and negative affect may be relevant to mixed affective experiences such as “kimo-kawaii,” although further research using construct-specific measures is needed to establish this relationship.

candidates.title: ARAM: a threshold model for understanding occupant acceptance of architectural robot adaptations
candidates.abstract: Physical interior elements are increasingly becoming roboticised to support occupant needs. Partitions, ceilings, and furniture can now physically and autonomously change shape or move to architecturally “adapt” indoor spaces, with the aim of improving occupant comfort, satisfaction, and wellbeing. However, occupants sometimes reject these adaptations when they are perceived as disruptive, unpredictable, or difficult to control. Motivated by the goal of making architectural robots more acceptable, we involved an interdisciplinary team of experts in human-building interaction, human-robot interaction, psychology, anthropology, and human comfort to qualitatively re-analyze how occupants accepted adaptations across three previous studies on robotic partitions. We found that an occupant tended to accept an adaptation when they recognized a personal need that the architectural robot was capable of addressing in a socially justifiable way. Accordingly, we developed the Architectural Robot Acceptance Model (ARAM), in which three qualitative thresholds along a continuum of perceived stress severity define four distinct acceptance responses to a specific adaptation. As the positions of these thresholds may vary across occupants and situations, ARAM supports testable estimates of how an occupant may respond to different appraisal states of personal need, adaptation capability, and social justification. Because architectural robot adaptations may simultaneously be experienced as robotic behaviors, building automation, and socially situated environmental adjustments, ARAM is particularly relevant to individual adaptations that enter occupants' spatial experience and may affect co-located others. We then discuss how the model can inform situated estimates of occupant acceptance of architectural robot adaptations, and outline how its broader relevance to other robotic, automated, intelligent, and smart technologies embedded in the built environment may be evaluated in future work.

candidates.title: Robotic Perception Systems Driven by AI
candidates.abstract: Robotic perception plays a critical role in modern robotics by integrating perceptual data processed through AI and ML methodologies to enable intelligent behavior. It underpins a wide range of applications, including object detection, environmental mapping, scene interpretation, human and pedestrian recognition, activity analysis, semantic localization, and object modelling. In this chapter, robotic perception is explored through the lens of machine learning algorithms that enable robots to interpret sensory inputs, learn from experiences, and make informed decisions. The rapid progress in machine learning, particularly deep learning, has significantly advanced the capabilities of robotic perception systems, making complex tasks and innovative applications increasingly feasible. Breakthroughs in human-robot interaction, autonomous decision-making, and high-level cognitive tasks can largely be attributed to these developments. This chapter highlights current trends, challenges, and emerging use cases that define the future landscape of AI-driven perceptual systems utilized in robotic platforms.

candidates.title: Assessing Cognitive Workload using Electroencephalogram (EEG) in Technology-Mediated Work Environments
candidates.abstract: Human–machine interaction has expanded rapidly with the growing integration of automation, robotics, and intelligent systems into industrial and training environments. Emerging technologies such as Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) are designed to enhance these interactions by providing immersive training, real-time task guidance, and enriched visual feedback. While these technologies have the potential to improve efficiency, safety, and learning outcomes, they also impose additional cognitive demands on operators who must process complex visual and spatial information while maintaining attention and situational awareness. In complex collaborative and immersive work environments, operators are often required to interact simultaneously with humans, machines, and digital interfaces. As human information-processing capacity is inherently limited, assessing cognitive workload is critical for understanding how operators respond to technology-mediated systems and for designing systems that better align with human capabilities and limitations. This research examines changes in operators' cognitive workload within three rapidly evolving technology-mediated environments: VR-based training, triadic human–robot-human collaboration, and AR-assisted teleoperation. Rather than relying solely on subjective self-reports, this research employs neurophysiological measures, specifically electroencephalography (EEG), to assess workload during task performance. To examine cognitive workload across these technology-mediated environments, three separate studies were conducted. Study 1 investigated cognitive workload among novice forklift drivers in a VR-based training environment. In a within-subject experiment involving 20 novice drivers, workload variations were analyzed across different task difficulty levels and repeated training sessions. Results indicated that both subjective assessments (NASA-TLX) and objective measures (EEG) effectively distinguished workload across varying levels of task difficulty. However, an additional training session did not substantially reduce the workload experienced by novice operators. Study 2 evaluated cognitive workload during triadic human-robot collaboration involving a teleoperator and an onsite worker performing a collaborative assembly task with and without robotic assistance. Thirty-two participants were recruited and assigned to either teleoperator or onsite roles. We also evaluated whether manipulating the task demands of onsite participants indirectly affected teleoperator workload. Findings demonstrated that EEG effectively detected workload differences across collaboration conditions and showed that robotic assistance reduced cognitive workload. However, no evidence of workload transfer from the onsite participant to the teleoperator was observed when the onsite task demands were manipulated. Study 3 assessed the effects of AR-based visual augmentation and material visibility on teleoperator workload. We developed an AR interface that overlays the real-time posture and position of the onsite participant onto the teleoperator's view. In a within-subject study involving 17 participants, workload was evaluated using NASA-TLX, EEG, and eye tracking measures under AR guidance and traditional multi-camera conditions, as well as under varying levels of material occlusion. Results showed that AR guidance reduced workload, while Occlusion level influenced EEG patterns and gaze behavior, suggesting adaptive visual information-processing strategies under limited visibility conditions. Overall, these studies demonstrate the value of multimodal approaches for assessing cognitive workload in technology-mediated environments. In particular, the findings highlight the sensitivity of EEG in capturing subtle variations in operator workload, with different EEG measures responding to changes in task demands and system design across VR training, human–robot collaboration, and AR-assisted teleoperation. While increased task difficulty consistently elevated workload, supportive technologies such as robotic assistance and AR guidance effectively reduced cognitive demands. These findings underscore the importance of integrating cognitive factors into the design of technology-driven systems to enhance human–machine interaction, improve operator performance, and support safer and more effective work environments.

candidates.title: HRI, Culture, and Social Anxiety
candidates.abstract: Culture and social anxiety are among the human factors influencing the social acceptance of robots. In this chapter, research results are presented based on comparisons among nations conducted by the author’s research group, consisting of those about attitudes toward robots, assumptions about and images of robots, Frankenstein Syndrome, and roboethics. Then, an overview of social anxiety-related research in the field of human–robot interaction (HRI) is provided, regarding on fear of negative evaluation and gaze impact, impact of social anxiety on anxiety and tension during interactions with robots, and effects of social anxiety on robot preference in dialogue situations. Finally, the possibility of interaction effects between cultural factors and social anxiety in HRI is discussed and some future research directions are proposed.

candidates.title: Disclosure willingness anthropomorphism and thinking style shape perceived fit and comfort in AI mental health chatbot interactions
candidates.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) conversational agents are increasingly used for everyday, non-clinical mental-health support, yet little is known about when these exchanges feel fitting and comfortable. We used a laboratory mixed-methods design to examine associations among perceived convenience of interaction (PCI), relational attitude (RA), willingness to self-disclose (WSD), anthropomorphism (AN), perceived fit/comfort (FC), and thinking style in 83 participants (43 rational-dominant; 40 experiential-dominant). WSD showed the strongest unique association with FC. A post hoc reverse model also found a unique FC-WSD association, leaving their temporal order unresolved. AN had no stable direct association with FC, but the WSD-FC association became stronger as AN increased. Group comparisons and continuous Rational-Experiential Inventory (REI) analyses converged: relatively stronger experiential processing was associated with higher AN, whereas relatively stronger rational processing was associated with higher WSD. The group-blind thematic analysis linked disclosure decisions to privacy, control, social distance, functional usefulness, and affective comfort. Together, the findings identify WSD as a key correlate of FC and show that anthropomorphism conditions this association rather than simply improving the interaction. Clear boundaries, controllability, and adjustable relational cues therefore warrant attention in future design research.

candidates.title: The Hidden Glue of Language: A Study of Discourse Markers with Special Reference to Functional English for Undergraduate Students
candidates.abstract: Discourse markers (DMs) are a crucial yet often overlooked element of effective communication. While undergraduate learners of English may possess solid grammatical foundations, their spoken and written output can still feel fragmented, hesitant, or overly mechanistic if they lack pragmatic tools to link ideas and steer interaction. This study probes the structural and functional roles of discourse markers within Functional English for undergraduates, with attention to group discussions, Just a Minute (JAM) sessions, letter writing, presentations, and everyday dialogue. Employing a descriptive mixed-methods approach rooted in classroom observation, evaluation of student performances, and a survey of fifty undergraduates the research centres on markers such as well, however, in fact, moreover, therefore, so, first, on the other hand, and by the way. Preliminary primary data show that 32 students (64%) utilized discourse markers effectively, while 18 students (36%) used them to a lesser or ineffective degree. Qualitative analyses of classroom tasks reveal how DMs contribute to coherence, transitions, turn-taking, politeness, emphasis, and logical sequencing. Illustrative examples from letters, group discussions, JAM activities, and informal conversations highlight the difference between linguistically correct but disjointed language and pragmatically organized discourse. The study advocates for explicit instruction in discourse markers as functional and pragmatic resources rather than treating them as optional connective words. The findings bear meaningful implications for Functional English curricula, classroom interaction, employability-oriented language education, and the cultivation of communicative competence among undergraduate learners.

candidates.title: Human-centric digital twins in industry 5.0: technologies, applications, and future directions
candidates.abstract: Industry 5.0 (I5.0) emphasizes industrial technologies that are human-centric, sustainable, and resilient. Human-Centric Digital Twins (HCDTs) support this transition by integrating worker data with robots, machines, tasks, and industrial environments. However, the relevant research remains fragmented across human modelling, Human-Robot Collaboration, Artificial Intelligence (AI), simulation, and Digital Twin (DT) research. Moreover, systems that use human data or adaptive automation are often described as human-centric without demonstrating measurable benefits to workers. This review addresses these limitations by distinguishing HCDTs from conventional human models, Human DTs, and collaborative robotic systems. It critically examines human-focused sensing, multi-modal data integration, biomechanical modelling, intention and motion prediction, robotic simulation, optimization, reinforcement learning, immersive interfaces, industrial connectivity, and data governance. Based on this analysis, a literature-derived conceptual framework is proposed that connects sensing, integration, human modelling, analytics, simulation, decision-making, adaptation, human interaction, and governance. The framework organizes the functional requirements of HCDTs and is intended to inform future system design and comparison; its practical applicability and effectiveness require further validation. The review argues that HCDTs must extend beyond worker monitoring and productivity maximization: human data should inform industrial decisions that produce measurable improvements in safety, ergonomics, wellbeing, autonomy, accessibility, or skill development. Such systems should also uphold privacy, transparency, uncertainty awareness, explainability, and appropriate human authority. By linking technological capabilities to explicit worker outcomes, this synthesis enables researchers and engineers to assess the human-centeredness of HCDT implementations and supports the development of trustworthy systems for I5.0.

candidates.title: Can there really be ethical robots for autistic children?
candidates.abstract: Abstract With the advancement of autonomous technologies such as AI-driven social robots, the academic discussions around ethical standards have intensified over the years. These discussions have resulted in increased emphasis on concepts such as safety, trust, privacy, human dignity and well-being along with variety of ethical frameworks proposed by scholars. In parallel with these technological developments, therapeutic interventions for autistic children assisted by AI and social robots have also attracted increased attention. Against this backdrop, this paper critically examines six social robotics projects funded under the EU’s Horizon 2020 initiative from an ethics perspective. The main aim of these completed projects was to develop AI-driven semi-autonomous technologies such as humanoid and non-humanoid robots to assist autism interventions. To address the ethical shortcomings of the said projects, this paper mobilizes perspectives from critical disability studies, critical autism studies and the autism community itself, particularly concerning the negative impact of interventions on autistic individuals as a neurominority group. Beyond the commonly addressed shortcomings in the field of AI and social robotics, the article highlights that the biggest shortcoming of these projects is the absence of critical reflection on the ethical acceptability of applying neuronormative behavioral interventions to a neurominority group. By situating robot-assisted interventions within the context of normalization and technoableism, the article points out the epistemic injustice and the harm that can be potentially enacted on autistic people through such technologically aided interventions. Ultimately, the paper questions whether ethical assistive technologies for autistic individuals can exist under these circumstances.

candidates.title: Ethical Considerations and Workforce Impacts
candidates.abstract: The rapid advancement of AI-powered robotic perception systems has raised significant ethical concerns and workforce implications. This chapter explores the ethical considerations and the transformation of human roles in an increasingly automated world. It begins by examining the ethical implications of robot autonomy, including decision-making challenges, accountability, bias, and transparency. As robots gain higher levels of independence, questions surrounding moral responsibility and societal impact become more pressing. A major focus is the evolving job landscape, where AI-driven robots automate repetitive tasks, leading to job displacement concerns. However, alongside these challenges, new opportunities emerge, requiring a shift in workforce skills and education. The chapter delves into the socioeconomic impact of AI, discussing job polarization, digital divides, and strategies for workforce adaptation through reskilling and upskilling initiatives. Furthermore, ethical challenges in human-robot collaboration are analyzed, particularly in workplace safety, trust, privacy, and regulatory concerns. The interaction between humans and robots raises questions about psychological impacts, data security, and legal frameworks, necessitating comprehensive ethical guidelines. The chapter also emphasizes the importance of preparing the workforce for robotic integration. It highlights the role of education in fostering AI and robotics literacy, the need for corporate and governmental intervention in workforce training, and the implementation of social policies such as Universal Basic Income (UBI) to mitigate economic disruptions. Finally, the chapter concludes with discussions on the future of AI-powered robotic ethics, emphasizing the importance of developing regulatory frameworks that balance technological progress with ethical responsibility. By addressing these issues, society can harness the benefits of robotics while ensuring fairness, security, and human well-being in the evolving job market.

candidates.title: Therapy as an NLP Task: Comparing LLMs and Human Peers Behaviors in CBT Sessions
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as ad hoc therapists. While prior research has found that LLMs outperform human counselors in generating single-turn empathetic responses, fewer studies have compared their behaviors across multi-turn sessions. In this study, we compare the session-level behaviors of human peer counselors with those of an LLM, both trained on the same manual to deliver multi-turn, single-session Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). Our three-phase, mixed-methods study involved: (a) an 18-month ethnography of a peer support platform, where seven counselors iteratively refined CBT prompts through 110 self-counseling sessions and 60 weekly focus groups; (b) a novel session generation method that allows direct, controlled comparison of human and LLM counselors under matched conditions—client responses were drawn from publicly available human-led CBT sessions while counselor responses were generated by a CBT-prompted LLM; and (c) expert evaluations conducted by three licensed clinical psychologists. Through data triangulation, our results show a trade-off. Human peer counselors use relational techniques to interpret subtle cues, adapt CBT to users’ values and cultural contexts, and use strategies such as small talk and contextually relevant self-disclosure to build rapport and guide the session, but often at the expense of session structure and therapeutic focus. LLM counselors, on the other hand, demonstrate greater methodological adherence to CBT techniques, but struggle to sustain turn-taking, frequently fail to distinguish between clinically important and trivial content, and are more prone to lecturing and imposing solutions. LLM counselors also tend to produce “deceptive empathy”, excessively anthropomorphic responses that can inflate user expectations of genuine human care. Taken together, our findings imply that while LLMs may outperform human counselors when generating a single-turn interaction, their ability to lead multi-turn sessions is more limited, highlighting that therapy cannot be reduced to a standalone natural language processing (NLP) task. We conclude by mapping concrete design opportunities and ethical guardrails for hybrid human-AI systems, emphasizing the risks of over-attributing human relational subjectivity to current LLMs.

candidates.title: Organizational Ergonomics in Robotics
candidates.abstract: The chapter introduces the organizational dimension of ergonomics for robotics. Specifically, it introduces the foundations of organizational ergonomics and sociotechnical principles for effective work systems design and development. It then highlights key challenges involved in issues related to work, activities, and quality of life in robotic setups. In this realm, attitudes towards robots and automation play a major role in the adoption of new technologies and change management in organizations. These broad-scale changes are important to be recognized as they shape human–robot interaction in various work settings, ranging from smart manufacturing to defence. The chapter then addresses specific aspects of teamwork and the design of high-performance teams. These topics include team performance and well-being, human function allocation, shared situation awareness, and job roles, amongst other such topics that will be explored later in the book by subsequent chapters. This chapter supplements the previous chapters on physical and cognitive ergonomics, but it goes beyond these aspects to highlight the organizational basis required to develop robotics holistically.

candidates.title: Ergonomics, Values and Robot Ethics
candidates.abstract: The development, implementation and use of technological artifacts introduces ethical issues—technologies are not ethically neutral. This ethical dimension is particularly obvious in robotic technologies, as many types and applications of robots are situated at the intersection of automation and social interaction. Consequently, developers, researchers and users of robots are confronted with ethical issues, for example concerning safety or (human) autonomy. With respect to ergonomics, two main themes can be identified: (1) Ergonomics itself involves certain values such as well-being, accessibility, performance optimization, safety, and trust. These values (and others) can and should be discussed in ethical terms. (2) Complex ethical issues in human–robot interaction are often difficult to address and can be cognitively overwhelming in the design process. One common ad-hoc strategy is to simply bypass and ignore these potential issues. However, professional tools that deal with ethical issues in the development and use of robotic system are available and may help to advance values in robotics. The most widely acknowledged framework to address values embedded in socio-technical systems during the development process is Value Sensitive Design (VSD). Focusing on ethical values, we present this framework with respect to robotic technologies. Finally, as implied by the very idea of human–robot interaction, robots themselves can be interpreted as subjects of action. This interpretation suggests an ethical reflection of the actions and behaviors performed by robots as if they were moral agents, an idea that is at odds with the key themes of ergonomics, values and ethics of robotics.

candidates.title: Human Factors in Robotics for Motor Rehabilitation, Assistance, and Prosthetics
candidates.abstract: Among the challenges in biomedical robotics, assisting and restoring motor skills is a priority to enable individuals with impairments to perform activities of daily living (ADLs). Robots can enhance human mobility and interaction capabilities through solutions tailored to individual skills, limitations, and goals in specific contexts. For rehabilitation, end-effector robots and exoskeletons are often programmed to guide users in exercises designed to restore motor functions after severe incidents, such as strokes, or in cases of chronic and degenerative conditions. These devices can also be integrated into telerehabilitation systems. Assistive robots, on the other hand, improve the quality of life for individuals whose impairments cannot be fully addressed through therapy, such as those due to aging. Devices like robotic arms, wheelchairs, walkers, and exoskeletons support ADLs and even facilitate social interactions through telepresence systems. Bionic prostheses, designed for limb replacement in cases of amputation or agenesis, could achieve a high level of embodiment–allowing users to perceive the prosthesis as part of their body. This need for a better integration between humans and robots exemplifies challenges common to all three domains. This chapter introduces fundamental aspects of cognitive ergonomics and human factors that designers, clinicians, and users must consider when using rehabilitative, assistive, or prosthetic systems. The ultimate goal is to provide a ‘truly’ human-centered motor assistance, and recovery, through robotic systems.

candidates.title: Analysis and generation of motion profiles from positive and negative human actions
candidates.abstract: Human actions convey not only their functional goal, the “what,” but also the manner in which they are performed, the “how.” The same action may be executed in a Positive or Negative manner depending on the agent's affective state. For example, handing someone an object carefully and politely reflects a positive manner, whereas doing so abruptly and dismissively reflects a negative one. This action modulation, known as Vitality Form (VF), is fundamental to human communication. Despite their importance, VFs remain relatively underexplored. This study investigates the kinematic signatures of Positive and Negative VFs in a pointing action and examines whether they can be reproduced through synthetic motion profiles. To this aim, kinematic data were collected from 40 right-handed participants performing three different pointing actions after recalling pleasant or unpleasant personal academic experiences. Each movement was assigned to either the Positive or Negative VF according to the emotional valence of the recalled experience. Several classifiers were evaluated for predicting VFs from wrist kinematic profiles, achieving a best accuracy of 73.97%. Grad-CAM analysis further provided insights into the kinematic basis of VF discrimination. We then investigated whether the kinematic patterns distinguishing Positive and Negative VFs could also be reproduced in synthetic motion profiles using generative models, achieving a Train-on-Synthetic, Test-on-Real accuracy of 72.50%. Finally, a perceptual study assessed whether the generated velocity profiles conveyed the intended Positive or Negative VFs. Participants identified the corresponding affective category with an accuracy of 75.80%, suggesting that affective information can be transferred to synthetic profiles and retained in a form that remains perceptually recognizable. Overall, this work advances our understanding of how affective states are encoded in human movement, demonstrating that these cues can be modeled, reproduced, and recognized in artificially generated actions. These findings have potential applications in neuroscience and social robotics, enabling artificial agents to recognize human attitudes and adapt their behavior accordingly.

candidates.title: Future of edge AI in biodiversity monitoring
candidates.abstract: Abstract Many ecological decisions are slowed by the gap between collecting and analysing biodiversity information. Edge computing moves data processing closer to the sensor, with edge artificial intelligence (AI) using AI models for data processing and selective data transfer. edge AI extends the scope of biodiversity monitoring by complementing retrospective ecological analysis with real‐time sensing, enabling responsive and adaptive decision‐making. However, the adoption of edge AI systems in ecological research remains fragmented because deploying efficient and reliable systems is complex. Edge hardware, on‐device AI models and network configuration are tightly linked, such that optimising any one component shapes the performance and feasibility of the others, demanding holistic system design. For the uptake of edge AI in biodiversity monitoring, it is essential to understand the design trade‐offs, performance constraints and implementation challenges faced by current systems. Here, we analyse 82 studies published between 2017 and 2025 that use edge AI systems for biodiversity monitoring across acoustic, vision‐based, tracking and multi‐modal sensing. We synthesise hardware platforms, AI model optimisation and wireless communication to assess how these design choices influence ecological inference and determine the practicality and longevity of field deployments. Annual publications rise moderately from 3 in 2017 to 19 in 2025. Across these studies, we identify four system types that represent distinct patterns of edge computing adoption in ecological monitoring. These include low‐power microcontrollers (MCUs) for single‐taxon or rare‐event detection ( Type I: TinyML ), single‐board computers (SBCs) supporting multi‐species classification and real‐time alerts ( Type II: edge AI ), distributed systems coordinating processing across multiple devices ( Type III: Distributed edge AI ) and network‐connected devices for cloud processing ( Type IV: Cloud AI ). Each type illustrates different trade‐offs among power consumption, computational capability and communication requirements. Our analysis reveals the evolution of edge AI systems from proof‐of‐concept to robust, scalable tools. We argue that edge AI systems enable timely and scalable ecological observations, but realising their full potential depends on closer collaboration between ecologists, engineers and data scientists to align AI model development and system design with ecological needs and field realities.

candidates.title: Foundations of Robotics
candidates.abstract: This book introduces readers to graduate-level study of robotics through an integrated, interdisciplinary approach that spans mechatronics, control theory, computer science, and AI. It is designed to unite students from these fields, equipping them with the collaborative skills needed to excel in robotics. It is structured around three core pillars: Mechatronics , Cybernetics , and AI . Mechatronics introduces practical tools and materials for robot building, programming, and design, covering open-source hardware, sensors, actuators, embedded systems like ESP32, and middleware like ROS2. Cybernetics explores feedback, control, kinematics, and dynamics, enabling the execution of complex trajectories for robots such as drones, mobile robots, and robotic arms, grounded in linear algebra and Lagrangian mechanics. AI explores modern transformer-based models, including GPTs and diffusion models, teaching robots to perceive, learn, and plan using Bayesian probability, neural networks, and PyTorch programming. Together, these sections provide a comprehensive foundation for understanding and innovating in robotics. Bridging foundational theory and real-world applications, this book is core course reading for advanced undergraduate and graduate students of robotics, mechatronics, and artificial intelligence. It is also a valuable resource for maker communities, equipping them with the skills needed to succeed in this cutting-edge field.

candidates.title: Personalizing Older Adults’ Cognitive Training Robot Games with LLM Support
candidates.abstract: As populations age, innovative solutions are needed to support cognitive health in older adults. This paper presents a platform that delivers personalized cognitive training games through a humanoid robot, leveraging a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate game content and users’ profiles from autobiographical memories. Four serious games were designed and developed as cognitive-stimulation activities, with content dynamically tailored to user profiles to provide personalised exercises. We conducted a four-week feasibility and user-experience evaluation study with 20 older adults (65+) and interviews with 10 caregivers to assess system’s usability, emotional impact, and perceived value. Results show that participants found the robot-delivered games engaging and emotionally meaningful, with significant improvement in perceived user control and high usability ratings. Caregivers especially valued the LLMs’ potential for scalable personalization. This work highlights the feasibility of integrating LLMs and social robots for cognitive activities in aging populations, providing indications on how to achieve this.

candidates.title: Large language model attributes and perceived moral agency of artificial moral advisors
candidates.abstract: Introduction: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as conversational artificial moral advisors capable of providing ethical guidance, moral reflection, and recommendations regarding complex moral dilemmas. Despite their ability to generate coherent and persuasive moral discourse, LLMs lack genuine moral understanding, intentionality, and reflective judgment, raising concerns that users may overattribute moral agency to these systems. Drawing on Theory of Mind, AI Moral Agency, and the Godspeed framework, this study investigates how perceived LLM attributes-namely anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, and intelligence-are associated with users' perceptions of agency and morality in the context of artificial moral advisors. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 758 valid respondents who were presented with vignette-based moral dilemmas relevant to young adults and instructed to imagine seeking advice from LLM-based conversational agents. Results: Perceived agency was positively associated with perceived morality, suggesting that users are more likely to regard LLM-based artificial moral advisors as morally capable when they perceive them as autonomous, intentional, and self-directed entities. Perceived LLM anthropomorphism and animacy were significantly and positively associated with perceived agency, with perceived agency fully mediating their associations with the perceived morality of artificial moral advisors. Perceived LLM likeability and intelligence were positively associated with perceived morality but were not significantly associated with perceived agency, suggesting that users may infer moral capability from social appeal and cognitive competence without necessarily attributing autonomy or intentionality to these systems. Discussion: These findings offer important theoretical and practical implications for the ethical design of artificial moral advisors, particularly regarding the need to prevent inflated perceptions of AI moral competence and authority.

candidates.title: World model for robot learning: A comprehensive survey
candidates.abstract: World models, which are predictive representations of how environments evolve under actions, have become a central component of robot learning. They support policy learning, planning, simulation, evaluation, data generation, and have advanced rapidly with the rise of foundation models and large-scale video generation. However, the literature remains fragmented across architectures, functional roles, and embodied application domains. To address this gap, we present a comprehensive review of world models from a robot-learning perspective. We examine how world models are coupled with robot policies, how they serve as learned simulators for reinforcement learning and evaluation, and how robotic video world models have progressed from imagination-based generation to controllable, structured, and foundation-scale formulations. We further summarize representative datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols. Overall, this survey systematically reviews the rapidly growing literature on world models for robot learning, clarifies key paradigms and applications, and highlights major challenges and future directions for predictive modeling in embodied agents. To facilitate continued access to newly emerging works, benchmarks, and resources, we will maintain and regularly update the accompanying GitHub repository on https://github.com/NTUMARS/Awesome-World-Model-for-Robotics-Policy alongside this survey.

candidates.title: Rethinking Robot Ownership: Comparing Public, Corporate, and Private Ownership Models
candidates.abstract: General-purpose robots, or robots that can autonomously and collaboratively perform a wide range of tasks, are almost universally imagined with a private ownership model throughout the robotics research and development process, in which individual households purchase, own, and maintain their own robots. In this paper, we argue that robot ownership should instead be treated as a central socio-technical design choice that fundamentally shapes who benefits from robotics, how robots are deployed, and which research directions become prioritized. We analyze three ownership models for general-purpose robots: private ownership; corporate ownership, in which firms retain ownership and provide access through subscriptions, rentals, or per-task fees; and shared ownership, in which robots function as community resources or public goods accessed through institutions such as libraries, cooperatives, or community centers. We examine how each ownership model structures access to robots and people’s relationships with them along key socio-technical axes including monetization, distribution, repair and maintenance, and liability for harms. We show that the de facto focus on private ownership risks entrenching unequal access to a potentially transformative technology due to its monetary, temporal, and logistical costs. More broadly, we argue that ownership assumptions quietly but powerfully shape robotics research agendas, contributing to hegemonic practices that remain largely invisible in funding, design, and evaluation. We contend that shared ownership is particularly promising for expanding access to robots and improving human–robot interaction, but that realizing this potential requires shifts in both research practices and policy frameworks.

candidates.title: Emotional attachment and problematic involvement with socially interactive AI: A critical narrative review of embodied and conversational systems
candidates.abstract: Background Socially interactive AI can elicit meaningful relational experiences. Studies often conflate attachment, anthropomorphism, companionship, dependence, and addiction, and group embodied robots with dissimilar software. Methods This critical narrative review of a reconstructed, non-exhaustive corpus ( Grant & Booth, 2009 ) is interpretive, not aggregative, because the initial search records disagree. We rebuilt the evidence set from the initially identified literature, separated primary from contextual sources, and sorted them by embodiment and dialogue architecture. Coding kept attachment functions distinct from related constructs. A reproducible OpenAlex and PubMed search (2010–2025) retrieved only one of the 12 primary reports. A coverage probe found 34 further provisionally eligible reports. We claim no exhaustive coverage or full PRISMA compliance. Results Reclassification left 12 primary reports and seven contextual sources. In these reports, relational significance appeared with embodied robots, non-LLM systems, and generative systems, carried by co-presence and touch or by conversational contingency, personalisation, and apparent continuity. Most measured companionship, trust, social presence, perceived support, or one problematic-use indicator. Few covered more than one attachment-system function. None established a behavioural-addiction syndrome. The predominantly cross-sectional, self-selected evidence cannot establish whether heavier use causes loneliness. Conclusions A relationship with an AI system can matter without amounting to reciprocal human attachment or behavioural addiction. Within the reviewed corpus, the evidence supports a broad, uneven continuum of involvement. Omitted studies may change the apparent mix of constructs, technologies, and outcomes. Progress requires longitudinal, technology-stratified studies with construct-specific measures that establish temporal order and impairment and separate embodiment from generative capability.

candidates.title: Cognitive Ergonomics in Robotics
candidates.abstract: Work tasks performed by humans within any work system are the connecting elements between humans and other system elements such as deployed technologies. Fundamental to any task performance are mental processes of those individuals acting within any socio-technical system. Perception, attention, learning, memory and reasoning are just examples of these processes. Within human factors, they are typically studied to evaluate, for instance, mental workload and situation awareness of technology users, whose errors can dramatically impact the safety and the performance of the system. Accordingly, this chapter presents concepts from cognitive ergonomics. These concepts should be considered within Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) studies and applications in order to assess and improve the design of robots which can interact with humans in terms of technology acceptance, usability, accessibility, and, overall, user experience. This chapter describes different effects on humans related to the interaction with robotic systems. Furthermore, specific HRI design elements and recommendations will be outlined. The chapter closes with an overview on quantitative and qualitative methods proposed to evaluate and to assess different aspects of HRI.

candidates.title: Comparing large language models and prompting techniques to control an embodied persuasive coach
candidates.abstract: Embodied agents play a crucial role in applications designed to influence user behaviour. Traditionally, crafting these agents requires considerable human effort. Large Language Models (LLMs) might open the possibility of creating agents capable of autonomous, open-ended interactions without labour-intensive development processes. We explore creating an embodied agent to coach users in real-time through slow and deep breathing exercises using an LLM. The LLM exploits a text-based context to generate a composition of predefined behaviours for interacting with the user through both verbal and nonverbal communication. This context includes essential details like the user’s respiratory rate to monitor the exercise. First, we assess the feasibility of this approach, showing that the LLM-based coach generates believable contingent behaviour compositions. Then, we conduct a 4 × 2 × 2 study evaluating how four different LLMs and two prompting techniques (reasoning- and learning-oriented) affect latency, appropriateness, and reliability of the behaviour compositions. Our findings show that more recent LLM models, combined with appropriate prompting techniques, improve appropriateness and reliability over previous models. However, our two studies also identify challenges, including latency, inappropriate feedback, and hallucinations. We discuss the limitations of using only LLMs to create persuasive agents capable of real-time user interactions, suggesting a need for hybrid approaches.

candidates.title: Building robots
candidates.abstract: Physical robots consist of sensors, actuators, computing components, and structural elements to hold them together. The hardest part of robotics for many newcomers has traditionally been the mounting of these components together to create actual physical robots. There are no widely agreed standards for structures and mounts, so most robots need custom physical components for making them fit together. Luckily, this has recently got a lot easier and cheaper. Improvements have been due to advances in 3D printing and open-source hardware standards. This chapter gives a tour of everything you need to set up your own garage mechatronics lab and mount sensors, actuators and embedded computers together in a robot body.

candidates.title: Interview with the AI: a quantitative analysis of AI companions’ relationship formation features
candidates.abstract: Abstract As millions of users increasingly incorporate artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots into their daily lives, scholars have begun to explore the relationships users form with these AI companions. Research on these synthetic relationships suffers from a lack of knowledge about the features of AI companions and how these features may contribute to the development of synthetic relationships. Guided by a theory-driven feature inventory that was based on stage models of relationship formation, this study employed systematic observations and structured interviews with the 20 most popular AI companions to determine how their features may relate to various stages in the formation of synthetic relationships. The results revealed differences between AI companions based on the distinct roles they fulfill. While friendbots displayed more features that are aimed at establishing new behavioral routines for users to engage with the AI companion, assistantbots had more features that integrate the AI companion in users’ digital lives to allow engagement during users’ established routines. The present work suggests that having features to support all stages of the relationship formation can theoretically make AI companions more suitable for intimate interactions.

candidates.title: GestAdapt: Workspace-Conditioned Co-Speech Gesture Generation for Humanoid Robots
candidates.abstract: Co-speech gestures for robots must adapt not only to speech and embodiment, but also to the workspace available for performing the motion. Since the same speech can be accompanied by different gestures, a robot can respond to workspace constraints, e.g., gestures for speech next to a wall. In these scenarios, the robot should gesture in a suitable motion rather than simply correcting an unconstrained one. To achieve this goal, we present GestAdapt, a workspace-conditioned framework that conditions co-speech gesture generation on a prescribed wrist workspace. The GestAdapt framework learns from six complementary co-speech corpora through a shared motion representation and supports retargeting to different robot embodiments. Quantitative evaluation shows that generated motions remain close to the real-motion distribution while respecting the workspace. In a user study, gestures generated under modified workspace constraints receive a mean quality score of 3.24/5, above our no-workspace variant (2.43/5) and below the reference motions (3.68/5). In a real robot evaluation, all compared motions are retargeted to the Reachy2 humanoid robot under identical workspace constraints. Motions generated with our framework rank first in 69.7\% of comparisons, higher than our no-workspace variant baseline and retargeted ground-truth motions constrained afterward. Overall, the results support adapting gestures to the available workspace during generation, rather than modifying unconstrained trajectories afterward to satisfy workspace constraints, potentially compromising gesture naturalness.

candidates.title: A System Dynamics Approach to Modeling Trust Dynamics in Conversational AI
candidates.abstract: Abstract Trust plays a central role in how users adopt and rely on conversational AI systems. Research shows that trust does not develop linearly or remains stable over time. Although initially it often increases, it can fluctuate, decline, and even collapse over time, even when the AI’s performance remains constant. Because existing approaches often conceptualize trust as a stable outcome or direct response to specific system cues, they struggle to explain these longer-term patterns of change. In this paper, we conceptualize trust in conversational AI as a dynamic self-regulating process shaped by repeated interaction and feedback mechanisms. Using a system dynamics perspective, we propose a conceptual model grounded in the "Limits to Success" archetype and implement it as a computer simulation. By offering a process-oriented and mechanism-based account of trust development, this work advances trust research beyond static approaches and highlights trust calibration as a dynamic, ongoing process with clear design implications.

candidates.title: CompanionSim: Synthetic Data for Evaluating Anthropomorphism in Human-AI Relationships
candidates.abstract: Many people now see AI systems as not just productivity tools but as social companions. Researchers are eager to study the consequences of AI companionship behaviors, such as validation, which evoke trust, empathy, and attachment in human–human interaction. However, human–AI interaction data is limited and unreliable, slowing research progress. We scale small amounts of real-world data by simulating multi-turn human–chatbot dialogue across a range of chatbot behaviors and use cases. We release CompanionSim: a simulation framework with 2,240 simulated human–chatbot conversations representing 16 chatbot behaviors across seven use cases. Human participants annotated the simulated conversations and real-world conversations in two experiments probing perceptions of companionship behaviors. We conducted Study 1 with a U.S. representative sample (N = 628) and Study 2 across the U.S., U.K., India, and Nigeria (N = 3,646). Surprisingly, we find that companionship behaviors reduced likability, humanlikeness, and trust in AI chatbots. These effects were larger in particular subgroups: women and older participants saw companionship chatbots as less likable, humanlike, and trustworthy. We encourage researchers to leverage real-world and synthetic data together to study the differential impacts of AI companions and to create benchmark evaluations of AI chatbots.

candidates.title: RL-Robotutor: a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for multimodal robot tutoring
candidates.abstract: Personalised robot tutoring requires real-time pedagogical decision-making under uncertain and multimodal learner states. Existing intelligent tutoring and robot-assisted learning systems often rely on static rules, single-modality learner modelling, or short-term correctness-oriented optimisation, which limits their capacity to balance knowledge acquisition, engagement, retention, and safe embodied interaction. RL-Robotutor is presented as a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that integrates cognitive knowledge-tracing signals, facial-expression and gaze-derived affective cues, and behavioural interaction logs through transformer-based fusion. A PPO-trained meta-policy selects among specialised modules for learner assessment, curriculum adaptation, strategy selection, and reflective feedback, while a hybrid reward combines immediate learning performance, engagement, long-term learning gain, and safety. The evidence is reported by source: five public knowledge-tracing datasets assess the cognitive prediction component; controlled simulator experiments assess policy learning, reward ablation, and multimodal fusion; and a randomised robot-tutoring study assesses embodied interaction with 120 undergraduate participants. RL-Robotutor outperforms rule-based, flat reinforcement-learning, knowledge-tracing, and LLM-based comparators. In the human study, the learning gain is 0.62, compared with 0.40 for the rule-based robot condition. The full hybrid reward improves simulator learning gain by 19% over correctness-only optimisation, and full multimodal fusion improves simulator engagement by 17% over text-only modelling. Jetson Orin deployment achieves 48 ms inference latency with an absolute AUC reduction of 0.007, supporting real-time edge execution.
